“I don’t believe this is happening,” Anna said, feeling worse.

Elsa’s eyes flew open. “There was something else. Wow, I just remembered.”

Was Elsa’s memory on the fritz, too? Anna didn’t dare ask her about her powers.

“What is it?” she pressed.

“In Ahtohallan. Our memories were missing. But there was something new in their place. One I’d never seen before. A memory of Sissel and Inger.”

Anna was startled. Ahtohallan held memories of the Vesterland sisters? She supposed that made sense—after all, the world was a lot bigger than just Arendelle. But could those memories hold a clue to any of this mess? “What did you see?” she asked, breath caught in her throat.

“I saw Sissel get swept away in the river, and Inger crying on the riverbank and calling to her,” Elsa said. “I know it doesn’t make sense.”

“No.” Anna’s hope faded. “Why would Inger be calling to her sister if she pushed her in?”

“I don’t know,” Elsa replied. “Guilt, maybe? For harming her own sister?” Elsa held her arms tightly around her chest. “It’s too awful to even think about, let alone see it. But the strange thing was, I didn’t call up the memory. It just appeared. Meanwhile, memories I know I’ve seen before—like of Mother and Father reading by their favorite tree—have disappeared. I couldn’t even recover them when I tried.”

“I think this is all Sissel’s doing,” Anna said, feeling helpless. She quickly filled Elsa in on everything else she and Olaf had read.

“So a draugr is almost impossible to destroy, is causing this strange weather, and might have stolen my powers and some of our memories,” Elsa summed up.

“And it wants to turn Anna into a draugr,” Olaf added, presumably trying to be helpful. He looked quizzically at Anna. “Hey, when’s the last time you saw your slippers?”

Anna felt the anger building inside her again. They had a lot of information and still didn’t know what to do with it. Luckily, she knew someone who might be able to help them. He’d been able to point them in the right direction before. Anna looked at her sister. “We have to go see Grand Pabbie and the trolls. Maybe they can help us figure out how to destroy this monster before it’s too late.”
chapters.zh:
克斯托夫或许有些事搞不清，但有一件事他记得很清楚：他爱吃越橘派。

把他和斯文交给能干的城堡厨师奥琳娜——她刚出炉一个热乎乎的派——安娜和奥拉夫便跋涉来到通往父母私人藏书室的密室。

安娜拉开水马雕像（它守卫着那个空间），书架随之转开，露出后面的拱形通道。

她和奥拉夫走进去。

沿着通道走向那间没有窗户的密室时，安娜憋住了一个喷嚏。

虽然她已尽力清掉垂挂在书架上的蛛网，里面还是有点灰尘。

在她发现这间屋子之前，已多年无人使用，成了蜘蛛和城堡里其他安娜并不想撞见的小生灵的绝佳居所。

但她把他们都赶走了，因为她知道母亲会赞成家里——每个角落——都干干净净。

她在房门口驻足，打量着塞满书籍、卷轴与其他奇玩的高耸书架——玻璃烧杯、银制天平。

一幅阿伦黛尔的阿伦（阿伦黛尔远古传说中的统治者）的肖像挂在远处的墙上。

这地方如今的样子，大概和他们父母十几岁初次撞见它时没什么两样。

据艾莎从阿托哈兰得来的记忆，这间屋子曾是伊杜娜与安格瑞的特别之地。

一个能独处、无人窥探的秘密藏身处。

一个坠入爱河的完美之地。

安娜为父母的罗曼史痴痴地叹了口气，随即回到手头的事，直奔书架。

她的手指掠过皮制书脊，寻找那本她记得读过的、关于夜里出没的神秘生物的书。

或长得像黑夜的白昼里出没的生物。

可它在哪呢？“出来吧，出来吧，不管你在哪，书啊，”安娜嘟囔着，盯着眼前所有的典籍。

它们的书脊上印着阿伦黛尔的历史传奇，以及土壤科学的资料，甚至还掺杂了几本有趣的悬疑故事。

却没有一本讲亡灵。

她叹了口气，挪到另一架。

它一定在这儿的某处。“我找到了！”奥拉夫终于从梯子顶端喊道。

他从最顶层抽出一本老旧开裂的皮面书，扔到地上。

书啪的一声落地，扬起一大团灰尘，呛得他打了个喷嚏。“它卡在一本讲奶酪历史的书后面。”他咯咯笑。“多‘芝士’啊，是不是？”他从梯子上跳下捡起书，拖到桌边。“就是它！”安娜看到书名《噩梦与水妖》时，如释重负地说。

她走到桌前，翻开书脊，在低矮昏暗的空间里，更多灰尘飘了起来。

她快速翻找，直到找到题为“亡灵”的一页。一幅衣衫褴褛、皮肤几乎要从身上剥落的可怕生物的素描，回望着他们。

安娜见了打个寒颤。“我撞上的就是这家伙，没错。”“‘亡灵，’”奥拉夫念道，“‘有时被当作鬼魂或精灵，其实是一具重新活动、腐烂的尸体，因未得妥善安葬而从死中爬起。’”两人对视，同时说了句“咦”。奥拉夫又道：“而且，这正符合阴森茜塞尔！

她是被淹死的，记得吗？”安娜想起那怪物在林中居高临下俯视倒地的自己、露出焦黑牙齿的模样，后颈一阵刺痛。

茜塞尔公主——死而复生。“继续念，”她压下恐惧说。“这里说亡灵能有魔法能力，能操控天气，把白昼变成黑夜。”她做了个鬼脸。“这个我们早知道了！”奥拉夫指向另一段。“这里讲的是记忆。

亡灵能在人熟睡时潜入，偷走人的记忆。”他翻过一页。“可偷拖鞋那段在哪？

那似乎挺重要的。”安娜心跳加速。“所以亡灵确实趁我和艾莎不在时来过阿伦黛尔。

还偷走了所有人的记忆！”“可为什么？”奥拉夫从书里抬起头问。

安娜皱起眉，双手攥成拳头。“我知道为什么。

茜塞尔在气我顶替艾莎当了女王。

她不知道全貌，现在就拿王国撒气！”她摇摇头。“我们需要找出的是，亡灵偷走的记忆是否永远没了，还是有办法找回来。

书上有说吗？”她焦灼地翻着页，字却仿佛模糊了。

就在这时，她才发觉自己在哭。“安娜，你还好吗？”奥拉夫关切地问。

她不好，安娜意识到。

她一点都不好。“要是他们忘得更厉害怎么办？”她忧心地说。“现在克斯托夫连我们的订婚都记不得了。

要是不除掉这亡灵，他最后可能什么都忘了……包括我。”说到最后，她的声音哽住了。

她无法想象一个克斯托夫不认得她的世界。

不再爱她。

奥拉夫拍拍她的手。“别担心，安娜。

我们不会让那种事发生。

我相信只要除掉亡灵，一切都会恢复正常。

看！”他指向书中下一页。“他们还列了办法呢。”“真的？”安娜问，心中升起一丝希望。

她快速扫过奥拉夫指的那段。

接着她皱起眉。“呃，上面说我们可以把它的头砍掉……”雪人耸耸肩。“够狠。

但多半有效。”“也多半不可能，”安娜嘟囔。

她回想起前一晚的遭遇，试着想象哪怕能靠近那具尸体到足以砍头的地步。“一定还有别的法子。”她翻回书，目光落在下一页的一段上。“好，这个怎样？

上面说若能引亡灵回到它的坟墓，它便会得到安息、消散而去。”“嗯，这确实没那么暴力，”奥拉夫赞同，显得松了口气。“除了……茜塞尔没有坟墓。

她被卷进海里了。”安娜努力不让自己慌乱。

这比她想的还难。“我在想，艾莎能不能把亡灵冻住，再把它碎成千万片，”奥拉夫若有所思。“冰之魔力……唰！”嗯。

安娜又查了查书。

片刻后，她摇摇头。“我觉得那也不行。

这里说亡灵对蛮力免疫。

事实上，书上说它们被激怒时，能诅咒敌人，使其无法变强。”她抿起嘴唇。“在森林里，艾莎筑起冰墙，把它气坏了。

紧接着，她的魔力就开始熄火了。”“听起来不妙，”奥拉夫低语。“是不妙。”安娜合上书叹道。“这简直糟透了。”“什么糟透了？”一个陌生的声音喊道。

安娜抬头，正好看见艾莎冲进房间。

妹妹双手撑膝，努力喘着气。“我收到你的字条，以最快速度赶来了。”安娜绕过桌子，张开双臂抱住妹妹。“真高兴见到你。

我们没来得及阻止亡灵。

它已经来过，偷走了人们的记忆！”艾莎一脸痛色。“不。

噢，安娜……你确定？”安娜做了个鬼脸。“很遗憾，确定。

连克斯托夫都……”她说不下去了，想起英俊的采冰人，满心苦涩。“还不止——书上说亡灵能诅咒敌人，使其无法变强。”她看着艾莎。“你觉得，这就是为什么我们见到亡灵后你的魔力开始熄火？”艾莎在丝绒椅上坐下，显得筋疲力尽。“也许。

我从阿托哈兰提取记忆也遇到了困难。

我那时不明白为什么。

可现在……”她闭上眼。“我真不敢相信会发生这种事，”安娜说，心情更糟了。

艾莎猛地睁眼。“还有别的事。

哇，我刚想起来。”难道艾莎的记忆也出故障了？

安娜不敢问她魔力的事。“是什么？”她追问。“在阿托哈兰。

我们的记忆不见了。

但取而代之出现了新东西。

一段我从没见过的。

一段茜塞尔与英格的记忆。”安娜吃了一惊。

阿托哈兰里存着维斯特兰姐妹的记忆？

她想这也说得通——毕竟，世界比阿伦黛尔大得多。

可那些记忆能解开这团乱麻的线索吗？“你看见了什么？”她屏息问道。“我看见茜塞尔被河水卷走，英格在岸边哭喊着叫她，”艾莎说。“我知道这说不通。”“是不通。”安娜的希望黯淡了。“如果英格把她推下去，为什么还会喊妹妹？”“我不知道，”艾莎答。“也许是因为愧疚？

因为伤害了自己的亲妹妹？”艾莎双臂紧紧抱在胸前。“光是想想就够可怕了，更别说亲眼看见。

可怪的是，那段记忆不是我调出来的。

它自己就出现了。

与此同时，我确信看过的记忆——比如父母在爱树下读书——却消失了。

我想找回都找不回。”“我觉得这都是茜塞尔搞的鬼，”安娜说，感到无力。

她把和奥拉夫读到的一切迅速告诉了艾莎。“所以亡灵几乎不可能被消灭，它制造了这怪天气，还可能偷走我的魔力与部分记忆，”艾莎总结道。“它还想把安娜变成亡灵，”奥拉夫补充，大概是想帮忙。

他疑惑地看着安娜。“嘿，你上回看见拖鞋是什么时候？”安娜感到怒火又在体内升腾。

他们掌握了很多信息，却仍不知该如何是好。

所幸，她知道有谁能帮上忙。

那人之前就指过他们正确方向。

安娜看着妹妹。“我们得去见皮比和地精们。

也许他们能帮我们在一切太迟前想出消灭这怪物的法子。”

sentences.en: KRISTOFF MIGHT HAVE BEEN CONFUSED about a few things, but one thing he remembered was his love of lingonberry pie.
sentences.zh: 克斯托夫或许有些事搞不清，但有一件事他记得很清楚：他爱吃越橘派。

sentences.en: Leaving him and Sven in the capable hands of Olina, the castle cook, who had a fresh pie hot out of the oven, Anna and Olaf trudged up to the secret room that led to her parents’ private library.
sentences.zh: 把他和斯文交给能干的城堡厨师奥琳娜——她刚出炉一个热乎乎的派——安娜和奥拉夫便跋涉来到通往父母私人藏书室的密室。

sentences.en: Anna pulled on the Water Nokk statue that guarded the space and the bookcase swung open, revealing the arched passageway beyond.
sentences.zh: 安娜拉开水马雕像（它守卫着那个空间），书架随之转开，露出后面的拱形通道。

sentences.en: She and Olaf stepped inside.
sentences.zh: 她和奥拉夫走进去。

sentences.en: Anna stifled a sneeze as they headed down the passageway into the windowless secret room.
sentences.zh: 沿着通道走向那间没有窗户的密室时，安娜憋住了一个喷嚏。

sentences.en: It was still a bit dusty, though she had tried to clear out all the cobwebs that had draped the bookcases.
sentences.zh: 虽然她已尽力清掉垂挂在书架上的蛛网，里面还是有点灰尘。

sentences.en: Before she’d discovered the room, it had been years since anyone had used it, making it a perfect home for spiders and other small creatures of the castle that Anna didn’t really want to run into.
sentences.zh: 在她发现这间屋子之前，已多年无人使用，成了蜘蛛和城堡里其他安娜并不想撞见的小生灵的绝佳居所。

sentences.en: But she’d shooed them all away, knowing her mother would have approved of a clean home—everywhere.
sentences.zh: 但她把他们都赶走了，因为她知道母亲会赞成家里——每个角落——都干干净净。

sentences.en: She paused at the entrance to the room, taking in the high shelves filled with books and scrolls and other curios—glass beakers, silver scales.
sentences.zh: 她在房门口驻足，打量着塞满书籍、卷轴与其他奇玩的高耸书架——玻璃烧杯、银制天平。

sentences.en: A portrait of Aren of Arendelle, the legendary ruler of Arendelle of old, hung from a far wall.
sentences.zh: 一幅阿伦黛尔的阿伦（阿伦黛尔远古传说中的统治者）的肖像挂在远处的墙上。

sentences.en: The place probably didn’t look much different now from how it had when her parents had first stumbled upon it in their teens.
sentences.zh: 这地方如今的样子，大概和他们父母十几岁初次撞见它时没什么两样。

sentences.en: According to Elsa’s Ahtohallan memories, this room had been a special place for Iduna and Agnarr.
sentences.zh: 据艾莎从阿托哈兰得来的记忆，这间屋子曾是伊杜娜与安格瑞的特别之地。

sentences.en: A secret hideaway where they could spend time together without anyone else watching.
sentences.zh: 一个能独处、无人窥探的秘密藏身处。

sentences.en: A perfect place to fall in love.
sentences.zh: 一个坠入爱河的完美之地。

sentences.en: Anna sighed dreamily over her parents’ romance, then got back to the task at hand, heading straight to the bookshelves.
sentences.zh: 安娜为父母的罗曼史痴痴地叹了口气，随即回到手头的事，直奔书架。

sentences.en: Her fingers flew over the leather spines, looking for the book she remembered reading one time, about mythical creatures that went bump in the night.
sentences.zh: 她的手指掠过皮制书脊，寻找那本她记得读过的、关于夜里出没的神秘生物的书。

sentences.en: Or bump in the day that resembled the night.
sentences.zh: 或长得像黑夜的白昼里出没的生物。

sentences.en: But where was it? “Come out, come out, wherever you are, book,” Anna muttered, staring at all the tomes in front of her.
sentences.zh: 可它在哪呢？“出来吧，出来吧，不管你在哪，书啊，”安娜嘟囔着，盯着眼前所有的典籍。

sentences.en: Their spines boasted tales of the history of Arendelle and information about the science of soil, and there were even some fun mysteries thrown in for good measure.
sentences.zh: 它们的书脊上印着阿伦黛尔的历史传奇，以及土壤科学的资料，甚至还掺杂了几本有趣的悬疑故事。

sentences.en: But nothing about draugrs.
sentences.zh: 却没有一本讲亡灵。

sentences.en: She sighed and moved to another shelf.
sentences.zh: 她叹了口气，挪到另一架。

sentences.en: Surely, it had to be here somewhere. “I think I found it!” Olaf exclaimed at last, from the top of the ladder.
sentences.zh: 它一定在这儿的某处。“我找到了！”奥拉夫终于从梯子顶端喊道。

sentences.en: He pulled an old, cracked leather book from the very top shelf and tossed it to the floor.
sentences.zh: 他从最顶层抽出一本老旧开裂的皮面书，扔到地上。

sentences.en: It landed with a loud thump, stirring up a large cloud of dust, which made him sneeze. “It was stuck behind a book on the history of cheese.” He giggled. “How cheesy is that?” He jumped off the ladder to retrieve the book, then shuffled over to the table. “That’s it!” Anna said, feeling relieved when she saw the title: Of Nightmares and Nixies .
sentences.zh: 书啪的一声落地，扬起一大团灰尘，呛得他打了个喷嚏。“它卡在一本讲奶酪历史的书后面。”他咯咯笑。“多‘芝士’啊，是不是？”他从梯子上跳下捡起书，拖到桌边。“就是它！”安娜看到书名《噩梦与水妖》时，如释重负地说。

sentences.en: She stepped up to the table and cracked open the spine, causing more dust to float into the air in the low-lit space.
sentences.zh: 她走到桌前，翻开书脊，在低矮昏暗的空间里，更多灰尘飘了起来。

sentences.en: She skimmed through it until she found a page titled “Draugrs.” A sketch of a creepy-looking creature in tattered clothing, skin practically peeling off its body, stared back at them.
sentences.zh: 她快速翻找，直到找到题为“亡灵”的一页。一幅衣衫褴褛、皮肤几乎要从身上剥落的可怕生物的素描，回望着他们。

sentences.en: Anna shuddered at the sight. “That’s what I ran into, all right.” “‘A draugr,’” Olaf read, “‘is sometimes thought of as a ghost or spirit but is in fact a reanimated, decayed corpse that rose from the dead because it didn’t receive a proper burial.’” The two looked at one another and said, “Eww,” at the same time. “Also,” Olaf observed, “that fits Sinister Sissel!
sentences.zh: 安娜见了打个寒颤。“我撞上的就是这家伙，没错。”“‘亡灵，’”奥拉夫念道，“‘有时被当作鬼魂或精灵，其实是一具重新活动、腐烂的尸体，因未得妥善安葬而从死中爬起。’”两人对视，同时说了句“咦”。奥拉夫又道：“而且，这正符合阴森茜塞尔！

sentences.en: She drowned, remember?” Anna felt a prickling at the back of her neck, thinking back to the creature towering over her in the woods while she lay on the ground, its blackened teeth bared.
sentences.zh: 她是被淹死的，记得吗？”安娜想起那怪物在林中居高临下俯视倒地的自己、露出焦黑牙齿的模样，后颈一阵刺痛。

sentences.en: Princess Sissel—come back from the dead. “Let’s keep reading,” she said, pushing her fears aside. “It says here that draugrs can have magical abilities and can control the weather and turn day into night.” She grimaced. “Well, we know that part already!” Olaf pointed to another passage. “And here’s where it talks about memories.
sentences.zh: 茜塞尔公主——死而复生。“继续念，”她压下恐惧说。“这里说亡灵能有魔法能力，能操控天气，把白昼变成黑夜。”她做了个鬼脸。“这个我们早知道了！”奥拉夫指向另一段。“这里讲的是记忆。

sentences.en: Draugrs have the power to slip in and steal people’s memories while they sleep.” He flipped the page. “But where’s the part about stealing slippers?
sentences.zh: 亡灵能在人熟睡时潜入，偷走人的记忆。”他翻过一页。“可偷拖鞋那段在哪？

sentences.en: That seems important.” Anna’s heartbeat quickened. “So the draugr did come to Arendelle while Elsa and I were gone.
sentences.zh: 那似乎挺重要的。”安娜心跳加速。“所以亡灵确实趁我和艾莎不在时来过阿伦黛尔。

sentences.en: And it stole everyone’s memories!” “But why?” Olaf asked, looking up from the book.
sentences.zh: 还偷走了所有人的记忆！”“可为什么？”奥拉夫从书里抬起头问。

sentences.en: Anna scowled, squeezing her hands into fists. “I know why.
sentences.zh: 安娜皱起眉，双手攥成拳头。“我知道为什么。

sentences.en: Sissel is mad at me for becoming queen in place of Elsa.
sentences.zh: 茜塞尔在气我顶替艾莎当了女王。

sentences.en: She doesn’t know the whole story, and now she’s taking it out on the kingdom!” She shook her head. “What we need to find out is whether the memories the draugr stole are gone for good or if there’s a way to get them back.
sentences.zh: 她不知道全貌，现在就拿王国撒气！”她摇摇头。“我们需要找出的是，亡灵偷走的记忆是否永远没了，还是有办法找回来。

sentences.en: Does the book say anything about that?” She flipped the pages anxiously, but the words seemed to blur.
sentences.zh: 书上有说吗？”她焦灼地翻着页，字却仿佛模糊了。

sentences.en: It was then that she became aware that she was crying. “Anna, are you okay?” Olaf asked, concerned.
sentences.zh: 就在这时，她才发觉自己在哭。“安娜，你还好吗？”奥拉夫关切地问。

sentences.en: She wasn’t, Anna realized.
sentences.zh: 她不好，安娜意识到。

sentences.en: She wasn’t okay at all. “What if their memory loss gets worse?” she said worriedly. “Right now, Kristoff can’t even remember our engagement.
sentences.zh: 她一点都不好。“要是他们忘得更厉害怎么办？”她忧心地说。“现在克斯托夫连我们的订婚都记不得了。

sentences.en: If we don’t get rid of this draugr, he could end up forgetting everything…including me.” Her voice caught on the last part.
sentences.zh: 要是不除掉这亡灵，他最后可能什么都忘了……包括我。”说到最后，她的声音哽住了。

sentences.en: She couldn’t imagine a world where Kristoff didn’t know her.
sentences.zh: 她无法想象一个克斯托夫不认得她的世界。

sentences.en: Didn’t love her.
sentences.zh: 不再爱她。

sentences.en: Olaf patted her hand. “Don’t worry, Anna.
sentences.zh: 奥拉夫拍拍她的手。“别担心，安娜。

sentences.en: We won’t let that happen.
sentences.zh: 我们不会让那种事发生。

sentences.en: I’m sure if we can just get rid of the draugr, everything will go back to normal.
sentences.zh: 我相信只要除掉亡灵，一切都会恢复正常。

sentences.en: And look!” He pointed at the next page in the book. “They even list ways to do it.” “They do?” Anna asked, a glimmer of hope rising inside her.
sentences.zh: 看！”他指向书中下一页。“他们还列了办法呢。”“真的？”安娜问，心中升起一丝希望。

sentences.en: She scanned the passage Olaf had pointed to quickly.
sentences.zh: 她快速扫过奥拉夫指的那段。

sentences.en: Then she frowned. “Uh, it says we can chop off its head…” The snowman shrugged. “Brutal.
sentences.zh: 接着她皱起眉。“呃，上面说我们可以把它的头砍掉……”雪人耸耸肩。“够狠。

sentences.en: But likely effective.” “And likely impossible,” Anna muttered.
sentences.zh: 但多半有效。”“也多半不可能，”安娜嘟囔。

sentences.en: She thought back to the encounter the night before and tried to imagine even getting close enough to the corpse to remove its head. “There’s got to be something else.” She turned back to the book, her eyes focusing on a paragraph on the next page. “Okay, what about this?
sentences.zh: 她回想起前一晚的遭遇，试着想象哪怕能靠近那具尸体到足以砍头的地步。“一定还有别的法子。”她翻回书，目光落在下一页的一段上。“好，这个怎样？

sentences.en: It says if you can lead the draugr back into its grave, it will find peace and fade away.” “Well, that does seem much less violent,” Olaf agreed, looking a little relieved. “Except…Sissel doesn’t have a grave.
sentences.zh: 上面说若能引亡灵回到它的坟墓，它便会得到安息、消散而去。”“嗯，这确实没那么暴力，”奥拉夫赞同，显得松了口气。“除了……茜塞尔没有坟墓。

sentences.en: She was swept out to sea.” Anna tried not to panic.
sentences.zh: 她被卷进海里了。”安娜努力不让自己慌乱。

sentences.en: This was proving to be harder than she’d thought. “I wonder if Elsa could freeze the draugr and then shatter it into a thousand pieces,” Olaf mused. “Ice powers…swoosh!” Hmm.
sentences.zh: 这比她想的还难。“我在想，艾莎能不能把亡灵冻住，再把它碎成千万片，”奥拉夫若有所思。“冰之魔力……唰！”嗯。

sentences.en: Anna consulted the book again.
sentences.zh: 安娜又查了查书。

sentences.en: A moment later, she shook her head. “I don’t think that’ll work, either.
sentences.zh: 片刻后，她摇摇头。“我觉得那也不行。

sentences.en: It says here draugrs are immune to acts of strength.
sentences.zh: 这里说亡灵对蛮力免疫。

sentences.en: In fact, it says that when angered, they can curse their enemies and prevent them from growing stronger.” She pursed her lips. “Back in the forest, Elsa made it really mad by making this wall of ice.
sentences.zh: 事实上，书上说它们被激怒时，能诅咒敌人，使其无法变强。”她抿起嘴唇。“在森林里，艾莎筑起冰墙，把它气坏了。

sentences.en: And immediately afterward, her powers started fizzling out.” “That doesn’t seem good,” Olaf murmured. “No.” Anna sighed, closing the book. “This is not good at all.” “What isn’t?” called out a new voice.
sentences.zh: 紧接着，她的魔力就开始熄火了。”“听起来不妙，”奥拉夫低语。“是不妙。”安娜合上书叹道。“这简直糟透了。”“什么糟透了？”一个陌生的声音喊道。

sentences.en: Anna looked up just in time to see Elsa burst into the room.
sentences.zh: 安娜抬头，正好看见艾莎冲进房间。

sentences.en: Her sister leaned on her hands and knees, trying to catch her breath. “I got your note and came as fast as I could.” Anna ran around the table, throwing her arms around her sister. “I’m so glad to see you.
sentences.zh: 妹妹双手撑膝，努力喘着气。“我收到你的字条，以最快速度赶来了。”安娜绕过桌子，张开双臂抱住妹妹。“真高兴见到你。

sentences.en: We’re too late to stop the draugr.
sentences.zh: 我们没来得及阻止亡灵。

sentences.en: It’s already been here and stolen people’s memories!” Elsa’s face was pained. “No.
sentences.zh: 它已经来过，偷走了人们的记忆！”艾莎一脸痛色。“不。

sentences.en: Oh, Anna…are you sure?” Anna grimaced. “Unfortunately, yes.
sentences.zh: 噢，安娜……你确定？”安娜做了个鬼脸。“很遗憾，确定。

sentences.en: Even Kristoff’s…” She trailed off, miserable as her mind flashed to her handsome ice harvester. “And that’s not all—the book says draugrs can curse their enemies and prevent them from growing stronger.” She looked at Elsa. “Do you think that’s why your powers started to fizzle after we saw the draugr?” Elsa sat down on one of the velvet chairs, looking drained. “Maybe.
sentences.zh: 连克斯托夫都……”她说不下去了，想起英俊的采冰人，满心苦涩。“还不止——书上说亡灵能诅咒敌人，使其无法变强。”她看着艾莎。“你觉得，这就是为什么我们见到亡灵后你的魔力开始熄火？”艾莎在丝绒椅上坐下，显得筋疲力尽。“也许。

sentences.en: I was having trouble pulling up memories from Ahtohallan, too.
sentences.zh: 我从阿托哈兰提取记忆也遇到了困难。

sentences.en: I didn’t understand why.
sentences.zh: 我那时不明白为什么。

sentences.en: But now…” She closed her eyes. “I don’t believe this is happening,” Anna said, feeling worse.
sentences.zh: 可现在……”她闭上眼。“我真不敢相信会发生这种事，”安娜说，心情更糟了。

sentences.en: Elsa’s eyes flew open. “There was something else.
sentences.zh: 艾莎猛地睁眼。“还有别的事。

sentences.en: Wow, I just remembered.” Was Elsa’s memory on the fritz, too?
sentences.zh: 哇，我刚想起来。”难道艾莎的记忆也出故障了？

sentences.en: Anna didn’t dare ask her about her powers. “What is it?” she pressed. “In Ahtohallan.
sentences.zh: 安娜不敢问她魔力的事。“是什么？”她追问。“在阿托哈兰。

sentences.en: Our memories were missing.
sentences.zh: 我们的记忆不见了。

sentences.en: She quickly filled Elsa in on everything else she and Olaf had read. “So a draugr is almost impossible to destroy, is causing this strange weather, and might have stolen my powers and some of our memories,” Elsa summed up. “And it wants to turn Anna into a draugr,” Olaf added, presumably trying to be helpful.

chapters.title: Chapter Eleven: Elsa
chapters.en:
BY THE TIME THEY LEFT the castle the next morning, it had started snowing hard, but Elsa knew there was no time to lose. They had to get to the trolls as fast as they could. They packed everything they needed for their journey into Kristoff’s sled, including Kristoff himself. There was no way Anna was going to leave him unattended for that long with his memory loss. (“What if he forgets what cliffs are and jumps off one? What if he eats poison mushrooms, thinking they’re ingredients for Flemmingrad stew?”)

Olaf insisted on coming, too, and so the four of them—led by Sven, who thankfully still seemed to remember how to pull a sled—headed out of town, toward the Valley of the Living Rock, where the trolls made their home.

The cold rarely bothered Elsa, of course, but it sure seemed to be affecting everyone else in the party as they made their way up the steep mountainside. And even she had to admit that she didn’t appreciate the snow and ice that had started piling up on the ground and making it difficult to maneuver the sled up the narrow trails—especially when it was practically pitch dark around them. The sun still hadn’t made an appearance, and if anything, the sky had gotten even bleaker since the lights first winked out two days before. Even their torches couldn’t seem to make a great dent in the darkness.

“Where are we going again?” Kristoff asked for the thousandth time. He looked up at Anna from his seat in the back of the sled, scratching his head. “Are we headed to the North Mountain to find your crazy sister?”

Anna groaned. Elsa could tell she was getting frustrated with him. “No, Kristoff. We already did that. Remember?”

“Yeah, of course I remember,” Kristoff replied. He peered at Elsa, who was sitting up front with Anna. “Who are you again?”

Elsa gave him a bland smile. “The crazy sister?”

Anna groaned again. “Please don’t make it worse.”

“I’m sorry.” Elsa put a hand on Anna’s knee and squeezed it comfortingly. “I know you’re worried about him. But it’ll be okay. I know it will. The trolls are masters at manipulating memories, remember?”

“Actually, I don’t,” Anna said with a sigh. “Since they took a lot of mine.”

“Right. Sorry. Again.” Elsa stared out into the dark night, gnawing on her lower lip. Way to stick her foot in her mouth.

“No, I’m sorry,” Anna replied, giving Elsa a rueful look. “I know you’re just trying to make me feel better. It’s just…this is so awful. I mean, look at him.” She gestured to Kristoff, who was staring at Olaf with frank fascination.

“Whoa,” he whispered. “Is that a snowman?”

“I’m Olaf,” Olaf said gently. “I like warm hugs?”

“A talking snowman?” Kristoff exclaimed. “Now that is just weird.” He turned to Anna. “Where are we going again?”

Anna moaned. Elsa pulled her into her arms. “Don’t worry,” she assured her. “The trolls are going to fix him right up! We just have to get there.” She peered at her sister’s face. “How are you doing?” she asked. “Are you feeling…fuzzy?” It was bad enough Kristoff and half of Arendelle had lost their minds. If Anna started going, too…

“A little,” Anna admitted, scrunching up her nose. “But definitely not as bad as everyone else. Maybe because we weren’t in Arendelle the other night, we escaped the worst of it.”

“And I don’t feel anything at all!” Olaf proclaimed. “Sharp as a tack! Smart as a whip! It’s probably because water has memory,” he confided to the girls.

“Strangely, you might be right…” Elsa mused.

“I usually am,” declared Olaf. He paused dramatically. “Or don’t you remember?”

“Whoa!” Kristoff exclaimed, peering at Olaf. “What are you?”

“Snowman. Talking. Yes, it’s weird.” Anna turned to Elsa. “Are we almost there yet?”

“Not really,” Elsa said apologetically, her eyes traveling down the steep mountain as the wind picked up, causing the snow to swirl around them and sting her eyes. Arendelle was so far away that it looked like a toy village. But they still had a long way to go. And by the looks of their shivering selves, she wasn’t sure they were going to make it without a stop to warm up.

It was then that she saw a light in the distance. Just a flicker, but something was definitely there. “What is that?” she asked, squinting. “Someone’s house?” Maybe if they were home, they’d let them warm up by the fire for a few minutes. She was pretty sure she still had a few marshmallows in her satchel, too.

Anna’s eyes lit up as she tracked the light. “No! I think that’s Oaken’s Trading Post!” She shot an excited look at her sister. “Which means…”

“Sauna!” they said in unison.

“Come on, Sven!” Anna called to the reindeer. “Last one to the sauna is a rotten snowman!”

“Fun fact! Snowmen don’t rot! They melt!” Olaf remarked as Sven picked up the pace, charging toward the light. From the way he was galloping, Elsa wondered if he might still remember Oaken’s usual carrot stash under the counter. Fortunately, the reindeer didn’t seem to be losing his memory along with everyone else. Maybe animals were immune, like snowmen.

A few moments later they were out of the sleigh and standing at the hut, with Oaken in the doorway, giving them a warm, welcoming grin. The burly redheaded proprietor was wearing an incredibly ugly-on-purpose Polar Nights sweater complete with a rainbow-yarn replica of the aurora borealis on the front.

“Hoo-hoo! Great to see you, Your Majesties!” he declared. “Real howler in December, ja? Come in before you freeze to death!” He opened the door wide, and they gratefully stepped inside the shop. The warmth hit them immediately and they all let out loud sighs of relief. Even Elsa had to admit it felt good to be out of the cold.

Taking off her cloak, she looked around. The store was all decked out for the upcoming Polar Nights festivities, complete with crates of Polar Night party kits, which appeared to contain an assortment of sparklers, special goggles to view the Northern Lights, and very silly socks. They didn’t, however, appear to be a very popular item: kits were piled from floor to ceiling. Which could have been due to the recent bad weather, Elsa concluded. Or…she surmised, glancing at the tag on one of the kits, maybe it was just the price….

“Come!” Oaken instructed, opening the door at the back of the shop. A blast of hot air roared into the small space, and they all sighed dreamily. “Let’s warm you up!”

A few minutes later they had all changed into white fluffy robes and packed into the small, steamy sauna. Even Olaf, thanks to his permafrost, was able to relax on the bench, a towel splayed across his lap. “Ahh,” he said, closing his eyes. “This feels just like summer.”

“Have I been here before?” Kristoff squinted at Oaken. “Are we friends?”

Oaken raised an eyebrow. “Is he all right?” he asked, turning to the women.

“Not exactly,” Anna said. “There’s something strange going on in Arendelle. That’s why we’re out here in this storm. We’re going to see the trolls in hopes they can clear some of it up.”

“Ja! I need this weather to clear up soon!” Oaken agreed, frowning. “I’ve had no customers for days! Usually this is my busiest season! But now—it’s like people forgot I was here!”

“There may be more to that idea than you know,” Elsa replied. “A lot of people in Arendelle have been experiencing missing memories, just like Kristoff here. It’s very strange.” She wasn’t sure she should mention the draugr. She didn’t want to worry the shopkeeper.

Oaken shifted in his seat, looking suddenly uncomfortable. “Well, that seems rather bad,” he said. “I hope my family is okay. They journeyed to Arendelle three days ago to attend the Polar Nights parties. I had been planning to join them once I sold all our party kits.”

“Might be time to have a sale,” said Olaf, looking at the large stack of kits, more of which were piled in the corner of the sauna.

“We can definitely check on your family when we get back,” Elsa assured him. “Once we figure out what’s going on.”

Oaken nodded solemnly. “And you think the trolls can help with that?”

“Sorenson seemed to think so,” Elsa said. “And honestly, we don’t have a lot of other options.”

“The trolls are very wise. Surely, they will be able to help you,” Oaken agreed. He paused, then added, “Did you know Grand Pabbie came here once? He bought all my spring mushrooms—at full price, too!”

He pointed to a wall of portraits across the sauna that Elsa hadn’t noticed before. Paintings of all the famous people who had visited the sauna, she guessed.

“Ooh! There’s us! And our parents!” Anna said, pointing to a cute picture of her and Elsa hanging next to one of King Agnarr and Queen Iduna, alongside other neighboring nobles. “Ugh. And there’s Hans,” she added, screwing up her face as she noticed the picture of her ex-fiancé—who was hopefully still rotting away in the Southern Islands. “What a bad likeness,” she added. “He’s really not that tall, you know. Or good-looking. Also, his nose is way bigger. And crookeder—”

“Is that me?” Kristoff interrupted, pointing to the next wall over, where there were more portraits—these under a sign that read BANNED FROM THE TRADING POST. Sure enough, there was a rough sketch of Kristoff, with an ugly scowl on his face, waving a fistful of carrots menacingly. Elsa stifled a giggle. Kristoff might not remember, but he and Oaken had a bit of an unpleasant history. Guess they were lucky the redheaded proprietor hadn’t left him out in the cold.

“Uh, sorry!” Oaken said, his cheeks turning red, as Anna shot him a look. “That needs to be updated now that you’re going to be a member of the royal family.” He leapt from his seat and ran over to the sketch, scrawling Okay! over Kristoff’s face in red ink. He glanced at Kristoff for a moment, then added For now! underneath.

Anna shook her head. Elsa smiled, going back to the original set of portraits to continue to look for Pabbie amongst them. Instead, her eyes locked on a portrait of two young girls, one with long braided hair and the other with a short bob. They had their arms around each other and were smiling happily. Something uneasy twisted in her stomach.

“Are those the…” she started.

“The famous Vesterland princesses!” Oaken finished for her. “Ja! They used to stop here with their parents on their way back home after trips. My father was only a boy back then, and they used to play together. He was always talking about how sweet they were. How close.” He smiled at Elsa and Anna. “Just like the two of you.”

“That can’t be right,” Anna interjected. “Sissel and Inger hated each other.” She turned to Elsa. “I’m right, right? It’s not my memory going on the fritz again?”

Elsa shook her head. “No. You’re correct. Inger hated Sissel because she wanted the crown for herself.”

“Inger wanted to be queen?” Oaken asked, looking confused. “My father said she wanted to be a scientist. He said she was always digging in the dirt and talking about soil.” He laughed. “My dad said it was quite boring how she’d go on and on about nature and protecting natural habitats for animals.”

“Inger was into protecting nature?” Anna asked. “That’s interesting. No one mentioned that to us before.” She glanced over at Elsa, and Elsa could practically see the wheels turning in her younger sister’s head. “I wonder if there’s more to this story than we know.”

Elsa shrugged. “Maybe. But first we have more important things to focus on.”

Like a monster on the loose. And missing memories. For now, the story of those two sisters had to take a backseat.

Elsa rose to her feet, wiping the sweat from her brow.

“Okay, warm-up over,” she declared. “Let’s go find the trolls.”

Elsa couldn’t be sure anymore whether it was day or night as they walked up the steep slope that led to the Valley of the Living Rock. They’d parked the sleigh at the bottom of the hill—no way was it going to make it up the last bit of that incline. Plus, it was so dark up here, they’d needed to buy new torches from Oaken just to be able to navigate the steep, narrow path without accidentally falling off a cliff in the process.

Fortunately, Olaf was enjoying himself so much at the sauna, they’d convinced him to sit this part of the trip out. He was hesitant at first, but the moment he and Oaken started singing Polar Nights carols, he’d decided it was for the best as well. Too cold out there! Nothing at all like summer!

Elsa had suggested leaving Kristoff, too, but Anna wouldn’t hear of it. The trolls were his found family—and experts in memory loss, too. If anyone could help him, it would be them. (Also, she didn’t really trust him not to start a fight with Oaken and get kicked out into the cold.)

They rounded the corner, stepping into the valley. Elsa was relieved to see the nocturnal trolls were awake and pretty busy with what looked like party preparations. The valley was decorated with moss and vines, and glowing crystals were strategically lighting up the space, giving it a beautiful golden glow. The trolls themselves were decked out in mossy capes—each one more elaborate than the last. There was even a very interesting sculpture of the famous Flemmingrad in the center of the valley, a troll effigy made of a mixture of mushrooms and moss residing above a foul-smelling pot of stew.

“Your Majesties!” cried a young troll, running toward them. He threw his arms around Anna’s knees, almost knocking her over in the process. He was small, but clearly heavy as a rock. “It’s so good to see you! Have you come for the Crystal Ceremony?”

Elsa immediately recognized Little Rock, whom they’d helped a few years back during his own Crystal Ceremony, a special celebration where young trolls earned their crystals by mastering skills such as tracking, harvesting, and stargazing.

“There are five trolls earning their crystals this year,” Little Rock told the group proudly. “And I’m helping the ones who are having problems. Just like you once helped me.” He peered from Elsa to Anna to Kristoff. “Did you come to help, too?”

Elsa shook her head. “I’m afraid not,” she apologized. “We’re here on much more serious matters. Is Grand Pabbie around, by chance?” She scanned the valley. There were so many trolls wandering about in the dark that it was hard to make out who was who.

Before Little Rock could answer, a new troll rolled up to the group and popped open. It was Bulda, the female troll who had raised Kristoff from the time he was a little boy. She was dressed quite fancifully in a long mossy gown strewn with colorful flowers. Her face broke out into a rocky grin when her eyes fell on her adopted son.

“Kristoff,” she cried happily. “You’ve come to visit old Bulda! And…” Her gaze turned to Anna and her toothy smile widened. “You brought your bride, too! Are you two fixer-uppers finally ready to get married? Because we can do it now! I mean, yes, we’re a little busy preparing for the Crystal Ceremony and all, but we will always make time for true love.” She beamed at Kristoff.

“Um,” Kristoff stammered, staring down at the troll with a confounded look on his face. “Who are you? What are you? ’Cause you look like a rock, no offense.” He scratched his head and started wandering aimlessly across the field. “Talking snowmen. Talking rocks…” Elsa heard him mutter under his breath. “What’s next? A talking reindeer?”

Behind him, Sven snorted. Anna face-palmed.

Bulda raised a bushy eyebrow, turning questioningly to Anna. The queen gave the troll an apologetic look. “Let’s just say he’s not exactly himself today,” she told the troll in a hushed voice. “It’s actually part of the reason we’re here. That and the strange weather.”

“Ah, yes. The weather.”

The group whirled around to find Grand Pabbie himself waddling over toward them. He was wearing his fancy ceremonial moss cape, and his neck was draped with so many crystals that Elsa found herself wondering how he didn’t tip over. He gave them a grave look.

“I was hoping you’d come,” he said. “I wanted to come to you, but this is a busy time for us, as you know. If we miss the Northern Lights, these young trolls will have to wait another year to earn their crystals.”

“And we’re sorry to disturb you,” Elsa said, dropping down to her knees to be at eye level with the troll. “But we didn’t know where else to turn. Something is very wrong in Arendelle. The darkness. The storms. People forgetting things. This is not your typical Polar Nights.” She pursed her lips. “We think it might be the work of a draugr.”

She paused, half expecting Grand Pabbie to laugh at her foolishness. To tell her what was happening wasn’t magical at all and that there was a very logical explanation for all of it. But instead, his face grew even more serious as he absently fingered a large red crystal hanging from his neck.

“A draugr,” he mused. “Yes. That would explain a lot. But draugrs don’t just come out of nowhere. When did you first see it?”

Elsa frowned. She and Anna had seen it in the woods on the way back from Sorenson’s. But Kristoff and Olaf had sworn they’d seen something the night of the campfire. The night Kristoff had told the story.

The night Inger had killed Sissel—fifty years before.

“We were telling scary stories,” she said. “And Kristoff told one about a draugr who was once a princess.” She bit her lower lip. “Do you think somehow we could have accidentally summoned a draugr by talking about it?”

“Names can have power,” Grand Pabbie agreed solemnly. “It could be that you got its attention with your story and angered it somehow.”

“I think it’s angry at me,” Anna piped in. “Though for a totally unjustified reason!”

Grand Pabbie cocked his head, seemingly perplexed. “What are you saying?”

“We think the draugr was once a princess from Vesterland who was going to be queen,” Elsa explained. “But she was killed by her younger sister, who wanted the crown. Anna thinks because she’s also a younger sister—who became queen—that the draugr wants to punish her, since she can’t get revenge on her actual murderer.”

“It’s true! It read the Village Crown story about me,” Anna added. “And then it started shrieking ‘Sister!’ Like, I’m the same as its sister.”

Grand Pabbie nodded sagely. “I can see why you might make that connection. But there is one important difference.”

“What’s that?” Anna asked.

“You did not kill your sister.”

“Oh. Right.” Anna looked sheepish. “Good point.”

“Draugrs are very simple creatures,” Grand Pabbie added. “They usually come back from the dead for one purpose. One unfinished task. One regret. Something about their past they hope to correct.” He leveled his eyes on Anna and Elsa. “Not to seek revenge on total strangers.”

Elsa let out a breath of relief. Well, that was something, she supposed. Though it didn’t really clear things up. “So why did it appear after we told the story? And what does it want?” she asked, feeling a little hopeless.

Grand Pabbie seemed to consider this for a moment. “Perhaps the stars can tell us something,” he said at last. Elsa watched, heart in her throat, as he waved his hand in the air and the clouds above them parted, revealing a shiny sky of stars so beautiful it took Elsa’s breath away. She hadn’t realized how much she’d missed the night sky in the last few days. The simple joy of looking up and seeing an entire universe shining back at you. The troll’s eyes took on a faraway look, as if he were going into a trance. After a moment, he opened his mouth to speak.

“What once did flee, now sets sail,” he intoned. “To end this all, you must tell her tale.”

“What?” Elsa asked, confused. What kind of riddle was that? “Do you mean the sisters’ tale? But Kristoff already told that! It’s what started this whole thing to begin with.”

“I’m afraid the answers aren’t so simple,” Grand Pabbie said.

“Meaning?” Elsa tried, but Grand Pabbie said nothing.

“Grand Pabbie?” Anna tried again. “What aren’t you telling us?”

Elsa watched as the clouds swept back in as quickly as they had parted, the sky growing bleak and black once again. The elder troll dropped his gaze from the heavens and turned back to the two queens, his rocky face as solemn as the grave.

“If you fail to set things right, day will forever be cast into night.”
chapters.zh:
等他们次日清晨离开城堡时，雪已下得很大，但艾莎知道一刻也耽误不得。

他们得尽快赶到地精那里。

他们把旅途所需的一切——包括克斯托夫本人——都装进了克斯托夫的雪橇。

安娜绝不可能把他这样失忆的状态单独留下那么久。

（“要是他忘了悬崖是什么，跳下去怎么办？

要是他把毒蘑菇当成弗莱明格拉德炖菜的料吃下去怎么办？”）奥拉夫也坚持要去，于是他们四个——由斯文领路，幸好它似乎还记得怎么拉雪橇——朝活石谷进发，那是地精的家园。

寒冷自然难得住艾莎，但在陡峭的山路上行进时，它显然影响了队伍里其余所有人。

连她也得承认，地上越积越厚的冰雪让雪橇在窄道上难以行进——尤其四周几乎一片漆黑。

太阳始终没有出现，而且比起两天前灯火初灭时，天空甚至更阴沉了。

连火把似乎也破不开这黑暗。“我们这是去哪来着？”克斯托夫第一千次问道。

他从雪橇后座抬头看着安娜，挠挠头。“我们是要去北山找你那疯姐姐吗？”安娜唉了一声。

艾莎看得出她对克斯托夫越来越没耐心了。“不，克斯托夫。

那事我们早做过了。

记得吗？”“当然记得，”克斯托夫答。

他盯着坐在前座、和安娜在一起的艾莎。“你又是谁来着？”艾莎朝他淡淡一笑。“疯姐姐？”安娜又唉了一声。“求你别添乱了。”“抱歉。”艾莎把手放到安娜膝上，安抚地捏了捏。“我知道你担心他。

但会没事的。

我知道会。

地精是摆弄记忆的行家，记得吗？”“事实上，我不记得了，”安娜叹道。“因为他们取走了我很多记忆。”“对。

抱歉。

又说错话了。”艾莎望着黑沉沉的夜，咬着下唇。

真是哪壶不开提哪壶。“不，该我说抱歉，”安娜回道，歉疚地看了艾莎一眼。“我知道你只是想让我好受点。

只是……这太糟了。

我是说，你看他。”她朝克斯托夫一努嘴，他正满脸新鲜劲儿地盯着奥拉夫。“哇，”他低语。“那是雪人吗？”“我是奥拉夫，”奥拉夫温和地说。“我喜欢温暖的抱抱？”“会说话的雪人？”克斯托夫惊呼。“那可真够怪的。”他转向安娜。“我们这又是去哪来着？”安娜呻吟。

艾莎把她揽进怀里。“别担心，”她安慰道。“地精会把他还原好的！

我们只要到那儿就行。”她端详妹妹的脸。“你还好吗？”她问。“你感觉……有点迷糊吗？”克斯托夫和半个阿伦黛尔都丢了魂已经够糟了。

要是安娜也开始……“有一点，”安娜承认，皱起鼻子。“但肯定没别人那么严重。

也许因为那晚我们不在阿伦黛尔，躲过了最狠的一波。”“而我一点感觉都没有！”奥拉夫宣布。“清醒得很！

机灵得很！

大概因为水有记忆，”他向女孩们吐露。“奇怪，你也许说对了……”艾莎若有所思。“我通常都对，”奥拉夫宣称。

他戏剧性地顿了顿。“还是你忘了？”“哇！”克斯托夫惊呼，盯着奥拉夫。“你是什么？”“雪人。

会说话。

对，是挺怪。”安娜转向艾莎。“我们快到了吗？”“还早呢，”艾莎抱歉地说，目光顺着陡坡下移，风越刮越急，雪在四周打转，刺得她眼睛生疼。

阿伦黛尔远得像个玩具村庄。

可他们还有漫长的路。

看他们瑟瑟发抖的样子，她不确定不歇脚暖暖身能否撑到。

就在这时，她望见远处有光。

只是一闪，但那里确实有什么。“那是什么？”她眯眼问。“谁家的屋子？”也许若有人在家，会让他们在火边暖几分钟。

她确信自己的行囊里还剩几颗棉花糖。

安娜顺着光望去，眼睛一亮。“不是！

我觉得那是奥肯的杂货铺！”她兴奋地看了妹妹一眼。“也就是说……”“桑拿！”两人异口同声。“快，斯文！”安娜朝驯鹿喊。“最后一个到桑拿房的是烂掉的雪人！”“冷知识！

雪人不会腐烂！

他们会融化！”奥拉夫说着，斯文加快脚步，朝那光亮冲去。

看它奔跑的架势，艾莎怀疑它是不是还记得奥肯柜台下常备的胡萝卜。

所幸，这驯鹿似乎没像其他人那样失忆。

也许动物和雪人一样免疫。

片刻后，他们下了雪橇，站在小屋前，奥肯立在门口，朝他们露出热情欢迎的笑。

这位魁梧的红发店主穿着一件特意做得丑兮兮的极夜毛衣，胸前还用彩虹毛线织了北极光的图案。“呼哈！

见到你们真高兴，陛下们！”他说。“十二月里可真够冷的，是吧？

快进来，别冻死了！”他大开店门，他们感激地步入店内。

暖意扑面而至，大家齐声舒了口长气。

连艾莎也得承认，离开严寒感觉真好。

她脱下斗篷，环顾四周。

店里为即将到来的极夜庆典装饰得满满当当，一箱箱极夜派对套装，里面似乎装着各色烟火棒、看北极光用的特制护目镜，还有非常傻气的袜子。

不过，这些套装似乎并不畅销：从地板堆到了天花板。

艾莎推断，这或许是近期坏天气的缘故。

又或者……她瞥了眼某套装的价签，揣测也许只是因为价格……“来！”奥肯招呼着，打开店铺后头的门。

一股热浪冲进狭小的空间，大家美滋滋地叹了口气。“给你们暖暖身！”几分钟后，他们都换上白绒绒的浴袍，挤进狭小蒸汽缭绕的桑拿房。

甚至奥拉夫，亏着他那永冻的体魄，也能在长凳上放松，膝上搭着条毛巾。“啊，”他闭着眼说。“这感觉就像夏天。”“我来过这儿吗？”克斯托夫眯眼看着奥肯。“我们是朋友吗？”奥肯挑起眉毛。“他没事吧？”他转向两位女子问。“不太算，”安娜说。“阿伦黛尔出了怪事。

所以我们才出门顶着风暴。

我们要去见地精，希望他们能弄清些眉目。”“是吧！

我巴不得这天气快点放晴！”奥肯皱眉赞同。“好几天没客人了！

平时这可是我最忙的季节！

可现在——好像大家都把我忘了似的！”“这想法背后的事，比你以为的还多，”艾莎答。“阿伦黛尔很多人的记忆都像克斯托夫这样不见了。

很怪。”她不确定该不该提亡灵。

她不想让店主担心。

奥肯在座位上动了动，忽然显得不自在。“嗯，那听起来相当不妙，”他说。“希望我家人的安好。

他们三天前去阿伦黛尔参加极夜庆典了。

我本打算卖光所有派对套装就去跟他们会合。”“也许该搞个促销了，”奥拉夫看着那一大摞套装说，桑拿房角落里还堆着更多。“等我们弄清状况，一定帮你打听家人，”艾莎向他保证。“等我们弄清怎么回事。”奥肯郑重地点头。“你觉得地精能帮忙？”“索伦森似乎这么认为，”艾莎说。“说实话，我们也没别的法子了。”“地精很有智慧。

他们一定能帮你们，”奥肯赞同。

他顿了顿，又道：“你们知道皮比来过这儿吗？

他把我所有的春菇全买了——还是全价！”他指向桑拿房另一侧艾莎之前没注意的一墙肖像。

她猜是来过桑拿房的名人画像。“哦！

有我们！

还有我父母！”安娜指着一张她和艾莎的可爱画像说，它挂在安格瑞国王与伊杜娜王后像旁，旁边还有其他邻国王族。“呃。

还有汉斯，”她注意到前未婚夫的画像，做了个鬼脸——但愿他还在南方群岛烂着。“画得真差，”她补充。“他其实没那么高，你懂的。

也没那么帅。

还有，他鼻子大多了。

还更歪——”“那是我吗？”克斯托夫打断，指向隔壁那面墙，上面更多肖像——挂着“杂货铺黑名单”的牌子。

果然，有一张克斯托夫的潦草素描，板着张丑脸，威胁性地挥着一把胡萝卜。“艾莎憋住笑。

克斯托夫也许不记得，但他和奥肯有过一段不太愉快的历史。

幸好这位红发店主没把他扔在门外挨冻。“呃，抱歉！”奥肯脸红了，安娜朝他递了个眼色。“既然你要成王室一员了，该更新一下了。”他跳起来奔向那张素描，用红笔在克斯托夫脸上潦草地涂了“好吧！”。

他看了克斯托夫一眼，又在下面添了“暂时！”。

安娜摇摇头。

艾莎微笑，回到原先那组肖像，继续在里找皮比。

不料，她的目光锁在两张少女的画像上，一个梳着长辫，一个留着短波波头。

她们手挽着手，笑得开心。

她心里泛起一阵不安。“那是……”她开口。“大名鼎鼎的维斯特兰公主！”奥肯替她说完。“是吧！

她们以前随父母回访时总会在这儿歇脚。

那时我父亲还是个孩子，常和他们一起玩。

他总说她们多甜。

多亲密。”他对艾莎和安娜笑笑。“就像你们俩。”“不可能，”安娜插话。“茜塞尔和英格互相恨对方。”她转向艾莎。“我说得对吧，对吧？

不是我记忆又出故障了吧？”艾莎摇摇头。“不。

你没错。

英格恨茜塞尔，因为她自己想夺王冠。”“英格想当女王？”奥肯困惑地问。“我父亲说她想当科学家。

他说她总在泥里刨，念叨土壤。”他笑了。“我爸说她翻来覆去讲自然、讲保护动物栖息地，无聊得要命。”“英格热衷保护自然？”安娜问。“有意思。

之前没人跟我们提过。”她瞥了眼艾莎，艾莎几乎能看见小妹脑子里齿轮在转。“我在想，这故事会不会比我们知道的更多。”艾莎耸耸肩。“也许。

但眼下有更要紧的事要顾。”比如一只在逃的怪物。

还有丢失的记忆。

眼下，那两姐妹的故事只能往后放放。

艾莎站起身，擦去眉上的汗。“好，暖身结束，”她宣布。“去找地精吧。”艾莎已分不清此刻是昼是夜，他们正沿陡坡走向活石谷。

雪橇停在山脚——最后那段坡它绝爬不上去。

而且上面太黑，他们不得不从奥肯那儿买新火把，才得以在又陡又窄的小路上辨路，不至于一脚踏空摔下悬崖。

所幸奥拉夫在桑拿房里玩得太开心，他们劝他这段路程就别跟了。

他起初不情愿，可当他和奥肯一唱起极夜颂歌，他也觉得这样最好。

外面太冷！

一点都不像夏天！

艾莎本也想把克斯托夫留下，安娜却坚决不同意。

地精是他收养的家人——也是治失忆的专家。

若谁能帮他，必是地精。

（再说，她也不大信他不会跟奥肯吵起来，被踢到门外挨冻。）他们转过弯，踏入山谷。

艾莎欣慰地看到，这些夜行地精都醒着，正忙着像是在筹备庆典。

山谷用苔藓与藤蔓装点，发光的晶体巧妙地点亮空间，透出美丽的金色光晕。

地精们披着苔藓斗篷——一件比一件精巧。

山谷中央甚至有一座很有意思的弗莱明格拉德雕像，一个由蘑菇与苔藓混成的地精像，立在一锅气味刺鼻的炖菜上。“陛下们！”一个小地精喊着，朝他们跑来。

他双臂抱住安娜的膝盖，差点把她撞倒。

他个小，却沉得像块石头。“见到你们真好！

你们是来参加水晶仪式的吗？”艾莎立刻认出小石——几年前他们曾在他的水晶仪式上帮过他，那是年轻地精通过掌握追踪、采集、观星等技艺赢得水晶的特别庆典。“今年有五位地精要赢得水晶，”小石骄傲地告诉众人。“我正帮那些遇到困难的。

就像你们当年帮过我。”他从艾莎看到安娜，又看到克斯托夫。“你们也是来帮忙的吗？”艾莎摇摇头。“恐怕不是，”她歉然道。“我们是为更要紧的事来的。

皮比碰巧在附近吗？”她扫视山谷。

暗处游荡的地精太多，难辨谁是谁。

小石还没答，一个新地精滚到队伍前，弹开了壳。

是布尔达，那个从克斯托夫还是小男孩起就把他带大的女地精。

她穿得十分花哨，一条缀满彩花的细长苔藓长裙。

她的目光落到养子身上，岩石般的脸上绽开笑。“克斯托夫，”她开心地喊。“你来看老布尔达啦！

还……”她的目光转向安娜，露出满口牙的笑更宽了。“你还把新娘带来啦！

你们这两个“待修理的”终于准备结婚了？

因为我们现在就能办！

我是说，没错，我们在忙着筹备水晶仪式什么的，但为真爱我们永远抽得出时间。”她冲克斯托夫笑道。“呃，”克斯托夫结巴着，一脸困惑地低头看这地精。“你是谁？

你是什么？

因为你看起来像块石头，无意冒犯。”他挠挠头，在场上漫无目的地乱走。“会说话的雪人。

会说话的石头……”艾莎听见他低声嘀咕。“接下来什么？

会说话的驯鹿？”身后，斯文喷了口气。

安娜捂脸。

布尔达扬起毛茸茸的眉毛，疑惑地转向安娜。

女王朝地精投去歉意的目光。“只能说他今天不太像他自己，”她压低声音对地精说。“其实这也是我们来这儿的部分原因。

还有这怪天气。”“啊，是。

这天气。”众人猛地转身，只见皮比本人正摇摇摆摆朝他们走来。

他穿着华丽的仪式苔藓斗篷，脖子上挂的晶体多到艾莎暗暗奇怪他怎么不栽倒。

他神情肃穆。“我还盼着你们来，”他说。“我本想去见你们，可正如你们所知，我们这阵子正忙。

若错过北极光，这些年轻地精就得再等一年才能赢得水晶。”“也很抱歉打扰您，”艾莎说，跪下与地精平视。“可我们不知还能去求谁。

阿伦黛尔出了大事。

那黑暗。

那风暴。

人们开始忘事。

这可不像你们典型的极夜。”她抿起嘴。“我们怀疑是亡灵作祟。”她顿了顿，半以为皮比会笑她糊涂。

笑她所说根本不神奇，一切都有合乎逻辑的解释。

可相反，他脸色更严肃了，无意识地摩挲着挂在颈间的大红晶体。“亡灵，”他若有所思。“是。

那能解释很多。

但亡灵不会凭空而来。

你们最初何时见到它？”艾莎皱眉。

她和安娜从索伦森家回程的林中见过它。

但克斯托夫和奥拉夫赌咒说，营火那夜他们也见过什么。

克斯托夫讲故事的那夜。

英格杀死茜塞尔的那夜——五十年前。

我们在讲鬼故事，”她说。“克斯托夫讲了一个曾是公主的亡灵的故事。”她咬了下唇。“你觉得，我们会不会因为谈论它，不小心召唤出了亡灵？”“名字自有力量，”皮比肃然赞同。“也许你们的故事引起了它的注意，还在某方面激怒了它。”安娜插嘴：“我觉得它在气我。

尽管毫无道理！”皮比偏了偏头，似乎不解。“你说什么？”“我们认为那亡灵曾是维斯特兰一位本要当女王的公主，”艾莎解释。“但她被想夺王冠的妹妹害死。

安娜觉得，因为她也是妹妹——且当了女王——亡灵想惩罚她，既然它无法向真正的凶手复仇。”“没错！

它读了讲我的《村庄之冠》故事，”安娜补充。“然后就开始尖叫‘妹妹！’好像我和它妹妹一样。”皮比睿智地点头。“我能理解你们为何这样联想。

但有一个重要区别。”“什么区别？”安娜问。“你没杀你妹妹。”“哦。

对。”安娜一脸窘色。“说得好。”“亡灵是很简单的生灵，”皮比补充。“他们从死中归来，通常只为一件事。

一件未竟之事。

一个遗憾。

他们希望纠正的、关于过去的某件事。”他把目光落在安娜和艾莎身上。“而非向陌生人寻仇。”艾莎松了口气。

嗯，这总算聊以慰藉，她想。

尽管并未真正解开谜团。“那它为何在我们讲完故事后现身？

它又想要什么？”她问，有些无望。

皮比似乎思忖了片刻。“也许星辰能告诉我们些什么，”他终于说。

艾莎屏息望着，他挥手在空中，头顶的云层分开，露出一片璀璨星空，美得让艾莎屏息。

她没意识到，过去几天她是多么想念夜空。

抬头看见整个宇宙向你回以星光，那份单纯的喜悦。

地精的眼神变得悠远，仿佛进入恍惚。“‘曾逃逸者，今启航，’”他庄严念道。“‘欲了此局，须述她事。’”“什么？”艾莎困惑地问。

这算什么谜语？“你是说姐妹的故事？

可克斯托夫早就讲过了！

那正是整件事的开端。”“恐怕答案没那么简单，”皮比说。“此话怎讲？”艾莎试着问，皮比却沉默不语。“皮比？”安娜又试。“你在瞒我们什么？”艾莎望见云层如分开时般迅速合拢，天空重归阴沉漆黑。

老地精垂下望天的目光，转回两位女王，岩石般的脸如坟墓般肃穆。“若你们未能拨乱反正，白昼将永坠黑夜。”

sentences.en: Even their torches couldn’t seem to make a great dent in the darkness. “Where are we going again?” Kristoff asked for the thousandth time.
sentences.zh: 连火把似乎也破不开这黑暗。“我们这是去哪来着？”克斯托夫第一千次问道。

sentences.en: He looked up at Anna from his seat in the back of the sled, scratching his head. “Are we headed to the North Mountain to find your crazy sister?” Anna groaned.
sentences.zh: 他从雪橇后座抬头看着安娜，挠挠头。“我们是要去北山找你那疯姐姐吗？”安娜唉了一声。

sentences.en: Elsa could tell she was getting frustrated with him. “No, Kristoff.
sentences.zh: 艾莎看得出她对克斯托夫越来越没耐心了。“不，克斯托夫。

sentences.en: We already did that.
sentences.zh: 那事我们早做过了。

sentences.en: Remember?” “Yeah, of course I remember,” Kristoff replied.
sentences.zh: 记得吗？”“当然记得，”克斯托夫答。

sentences.en: He peered at Elsa, who was sitting up front with Anna. “Who are you again?” Elsa gave him a bland smile. “The crazy sister?” Anna groaned again. “Please don’t make it worse.” “I’m sorry.” Elsa put a hand on Anna’s knee and squeezed it comfortingly. “I know you’re worried about him.
sentences.zh: 他盯着坐在前座、和安娜在一起的艾莎。“你又是谁来着？”艾莎朝他淡淡一笑。“疯姐姐？”安娜又唉了一声。“求你别添乱了。”“抱歉。”艾莎把手放到安娜膝上，安抚地捏了捏。“我知道你担心他。

sentences.en: But it’ll be okay.
sentences.zh: 但会没事的。

sentences.en: I know it will.
sentences.zh: 我知道会。

sentences.en: The trolls are masters at manipulating memories, remember?” “Actually, I don’t,” Anna said with a sigh. “Since they took a lot of mine.” “Right.
sentences.zh: 地精是摆弄记忆的行家，记得吗？”“事实上，我不记得了，”安娜叹道。“因为他们取走了我很多记忆。”“对。

sentences.en: Sorry.
sentences.zh: 抱歉。

sentences.en: Again.” Elsa stared out into the dark night, gnawing on her lower lip.
sentences.zh: 又说错话了。”艾莎望着黑沉沉的夜，咬着下唇。

sentences.en: Way to stick her foot in her mouth. “No, I’m sorry,” Anna replied, giving Elsa a rueful look. “I know you’re just trying to make me feel better.
sentences.zh: 真是哪壶不开提哪壶。“不，该我说抱歉，”安娜回道，歉疚地看了艾莎一眼。“我知道你只是想让我好受点。

sentences.en: It’s just…this is so awful.
sentences.zh: 只是……这太糟了。

sentences.en: I mean, look at him.” She gestured to Kristoff, who was staring at Olaf with frank fascination. “Whoa,” he whispered. “Is that a snowman?” “I’m Olaf,” Olaf said gently. “I like warm hugs?” “A talking snowman?” Kristoff exclaimed. “Now that is just weird.” He turned to Anna. “Where are we going again?” Anna moaned.
sentences.zh: 我是说，你看他。”她朝克斯托夫一努嘴，他正满脸新鲜劲儿地盯着奥拉夫。“哇，”他低语。“那是雪人吗？”“我是奥拉夫，”奥拉夫温和地说。“我喜欢温暖的抱抱？”“会说话的雪人？”克斯托夫惊呼。“那可真够怪的。”他转向安娜。“我们这又是去哪来着？”安娜呻吟。

sentences.en: Elsa pulled her into her arms. “Don’t worry,” she assured her. “The trolls are going to fix him right up!
sentences.zh: 艾莎把她揽进怀里。“别担心，”她安慰道。“地精会把他还原好的！

sentences.en: We just have to get there.” She peered at her sister’s face. “How are you doing?” she asked. “Are you feeling…fuzzy?” It was bad enough Kristoff and half of Arendelle had lost their minds.
sentences.zh: 我们只要到那儿就行。”她端详妹妹的脸。“你还好吗？”她问。“你感觉……有点迷糊吗？”克斯托夫和半个阿伦黛尔都丢了魂已经够糟了。

sentences.en: If Anna started going, too… “A little,” Anna admitted, scrunching up her nose. “But definitely not as bad as everyone else.
sentences.zh: 要是安娜也开始……“有一点，”安娜承认，皱起鼻子。“但肯定没别人那么严重。

sentences.zh: 也许因为那晚我们不在阿伦黛尔，躲过了最狠的一波。”“而我一点感觉都没有！”奥拉夫宣布。“清醒得很！

sentences.en: Smart as a whip!
sentences.zh: 机灵得很！

sentences.en: It’s probably because water has memory,” he confided to the girls. “Strangely, you might be right…” Elsa mused. “I usually am,” declared Olaf.
sentences.zh: 大概因为水有记忆，”他向女孩们吐露。“奇怪，你也许说对了……”艾莎若有所思。“我通常都对，”奥拉夫宣称。

sentences.en: He paused dramatically. “Or don’t you remember ?” “Whoa!” Kristoff exclaimed, peering at Olaf. “What are you?” “Snowman.
sentences.zh: 他戏剧性地顿了顿。“还是你忘了？”“哇！”克斯托夫惊呼，盯着奥拉夫。“你是什么？”“雪人。

sentences.en: Talking.
sentences.zh: 会说话。

sentences.en: Yes, it’s weird.” Anna turned to Elsa. “Are we almost there yet?” “Not really,” Elsa said apologetically, her eyes traveling down the steep mountain as the wind picked up, causing the snow to swirl around them and sting her eyes.
sentences.zh: 对，是挺怪。”安娜转向艾莎。“我们快到了吗？”“还早呢，”艾莎抱歉地说，目光顺着陡坡下移，风越刮越急，雪在四周打转，刺得她眼睛生疼。

sentences.en: Arendelle was so far away that it looked like a toy village.
sentences.zh: 阿伦黛尔远得像个玩具村庄。

sentences.en: But they still had a long way to go.
sentences.zh: 可他们还有漫长的路。

sentences.en: And by the looks of their shivering selves, she wasn’t sure they were going to make it without a stop to warm up.
sentences.zh: 看他们瑟瑟发抖的样子，她不确定不歇脚暖暖身能否撑到。

sentences.zh: 就在这时，她望见远处有光。

sentences.zh: 只是一闪，但那里确实有什么。“那是什么？”她眯眼问。“谁家的屋子？”也许若有人在家，会让他们在火边暖几分钟。

sentences.en: She was pretty sure she still had a few marshmallows in her satchel, too.
sentences.zh: 她确信自己的行囊里还剩几颗棉花糖。

sentences.zh: 安娜顺着光望去，眼睛一亮。“不是！

sentences.zh: 雪人不会腐烂！

sentences.en: They melt!” Olaf remarked as Sven picked up the pace, charging toward the light.
sentences.zh: 他们会融化！”奥拉夫说着，斯文加快脚步，朝那光亮冲去。

sentences.zh: 看它奔跑的架势，艾莎怀疑它是不是还记得奥肯柜台下常备的胡萝卜。

sentences.en: Fortunately, the reindeer didn’t seem to be losing his memory along with everyone else.
sentences.zh: 所幸，这驯鹿似乎没像其他人那样失忆。

sentences.en: Maybe animals were immune, like snowmen.
sentences.zh: 也许动物和雪人一样免疫。

sentences.zh: 片刻后，他们下了雪橇，站在小屋前，奥肯立在门口，朝他们露出热情欢迎的笑。

sentences.zh: 这位魁梧的红发店主穿着一件特意做得丑兮兮的极夜毛衣，胸前还用彩虹毛线织了北极光的图案。“呼哈！

sentences.en: Great to see you, Your Majesties!” he declared. “Real howler in December, ja ?
sentences.zh: 见到你们真高兴，陛下们！”他说。“十二月里可真够冷的，是吧？

sentences.en: Come in before you freeze to death!” He opened the door wide, and they gratefully stepped inside the shop.
sentences.zh: 快进来，别冻死了！”他大开店门，他们感激地步入店内。

sentences.en: The warmth hit them immediately and they all let out loud sighs of relief.
sentences.zh: 暖意扑面而至，大家齐声舒了口长气。

sentences.en: Even Elsa had to admit it felt good to be out of the cold.
sentences.zh: 连艾莎也得承认，离开严寒感觉真好。

sentences.en: Taking off her cloak, she looked around.
sentences.zh: 她脱下斗篷，环顾四周。

sentences.zh: 店里为即将到来的极夜庆典装饰得满满当当，一箱箱极夜派对套装，里面似乎装着各色烟火棒、看北极光用的特制护目镜，还有非常傻气的袜子。

sentences.en: They didn’t, however, appear to be a very popular item: kits were piled from floor to ceiling.
sentences.zh: 不过，这些套装似乎并不畅销：从地板堆到了天花板。

sentences.en: Which could have been due to the recent bad weather, Elsa concluded.
sentences.zh: 艾莎推断，这或许是近期坏天气的缘故。

sentences.en: Or…she surmised, glancing at the tag on one of the kits, maybe it was just the price…. “Come!” Oaken instructed, opening the door at the back of the shop.
sentences.zh: 又或者……她瞥了眼某套装的价签，揣测也许只是因为价格……“来！”奥肯招呼着，打开店铺后头的门。

sentences.en: A blast of hot air roared into the small space, and they all sighed dreamily. “Let’s warm you up!” A few minutes later they had all changed into white fluffy robes and packed into the small, steamy sauna.
sentences.zh: 一股热浪冲进狭小的空间，大家美滋滋地叹了口气。“给你们暖暖身！”几分钟后，他们都换上白绒绒的浴袍，挤进狭小蒸汽缭绕的桑拿房。

sentences.en: Even Olaf, thanks to his permafrost, was able to relax on the bench, a towel splayed across his lap. “Ahh,” he said, closing his eyes. “This feels just like summer.” “Have I been here before?” Kristoff squinted at Oaken. “Are we friends?” Oaken raised an eyebrow. “Is he all right?” he asked, turning to the women. “Not exactly,” Anna said. “There’s something strange going on in Arendelle.
sentences.zh: 甚至奥拉夫，亏着他那永冻的体魄，也能在长凳上放松，膝上搭着条毛巾。“啊，”他闭着眼说。“这感觉就像夏天。”“我来过这儿吗？”克斯托夫眯眼看着奥肯。“我们是朋友吗？”奥肯挑起眉毛。“他没事吧？”他转向两位女子问。“不太算，”安娜说。“阿伦黛尔出了怪事。

sentences.en: That’s why we’re out here in this storm.
sentences.zh: 所以我们才出门顶着风暴。

sentences.en: We’re going to see the trolls in hopes they can clear some of it up.” “ Ja!
sentences.zh: 我们要去见地精，希望他们能弄清些眉目。”“是吧！

sentences.en: I need this weather to clear up soon!” Oaken agreed, frowning. “I’ve had no customers for days!
sentences.zh: 我巴不得这天气快点放晴！”奥肯皱眉赞同。“好几天没客人了！

sentences.en: Usually this is my busiest season!
sentences.zh: 平时这可是我最忙的季节！

sentences.en: It’s very strange.” She wasn’t sure she should mention the draugr.
sentences.zh: 很怪。”她不确定该不该提亡灵。

sentences.en: She didn’t want to worry the shopkeeper.
sentences.zh: 她不想让店主担心。

sentences.zh: 奥肯在座位上动了动，忽然显得不自在。“嗯，那听起来相当不妙，”他说。“希望我家人的安好。

sentences.en: They journeyed to Arendelle three days ago to attend the Polar Nights parties.
sentences.zh: 他们三天前去阿伦黛尔参加极夜庆典了。

sentences.en: I had been planning to join them once I sold all our party kits.” “Might be time to have a sale,” said Olaf, looking at the large stack of kits, more of which were piled in the corner of the sauna. “We can definitely check on your family when we get back,” Elsa assured him. “Once we figure out what’s going on.” Oaken nodded solemnly. “And you think the trolls can help with that?” “Sorenson seemed to think so,” Elsa said. “And honestly, we don’t have a lot of other options.” “The trolls are very wise.
sentences.zh: 我本打算卖光所有派对套装就去跟他们会合。”“也许该搞个促销了，”奥拉夫看着那一大摞套装说，桑拿房角落里还堆着更多。“等我们弄清状况，一定帮你打听家人，”艾莎向他保证。“等我们弄清怎么回事。”奥肯郑重地点头。“你觉得地精能帮忙？”“索伦森似乎这么认为，”艾莎说。“说实话，我们也没别的法子了。”“地精很有智慧。

sentences.en: Surely, they will be able to help you,” Oaken agreed.
sentences.zh: 他们一定能帮你们，”奥肯赞同。

sentences.zh: 他顿了顿，又道：“你们知道皮比来过这儿吗？

sentences.zh: 还有汉斯，”她注意到前未婚夫的画像，做了个鬼脸——但愿他还在南方群岛烂着。“画得真差，”她补充。“他其实没那么高，你懂的。

sentences.en: Or good-looking.

sentences.en: Sure enough, there was a rough sketch of Kristoff, with an ugly scowl on his face, waving a fistful of carrots menacingly.

sentences.zh: 克斯托夫也许不记得，但他和奥肯有过一段不太愉快的历史。

sentences.zh: 多亲密。”他对艾莎和安娜笑笑。“就像你们俩。”“不可能，”安娜插话。“茜塞尔和英格互相恨对方。”她转向艾莎。“我说得对吧，对吧？

chapters.title: Chapter Twelve: Anna
chapters.en:
ANNA WAS TOO STUNNED TO SPEAK.

She couldn’t believe what she was hearing. Forever night? The kingdom plunged into eternal darkness? Not to mention never-ending storms! What would they do if that happened? Without the sun, Arendelle’s crops would wither and die. Ships would sink in the stormy waters of the sea instead of reaching safe harbor with their medicines and supplies. She didn’t want to believe what Grand Pabbie was saying, but he’d never been wrong about something like this.

And then there was another horrifying question needling at her, begging for an answer. One she wasn’t sure she really wanted to ask. Because while storms were bad and eternal night was worse…

Memories…people’s memories…

“Grand Pabbie?” she ventured, her tone softening. “If we can’t rid Arendelle of this threat—”

“We will,” Elsa cut in firmly.

“But if we can’t,” Anna continued gently, “does that mean…could it also mean…”

Her voice caught as she stared across the valley at the burly ice harvester and his reindeer. Kristoff was taking in the sight of the talking, rolling, jumping trolls in amazement, as if he’d never seen them before. Even Sven was looking at him strangely. “Will the people…will Kristoff…”

“I’m sorry, Anna,” Grand Pabbie replied, his voice equally soft. He didn’t have to continue.

Anna forced herself to focus on the crystals around the trolls’ necks, hoping the illuminating colors would calm her. All she wanted to do was scream. Why did Kristoff have to tell that scary story? Why?

“But you must know some spell, or remedy, that can help people with their lost memories,” she insisted, her voice escalating in volume. “You’ve removed memories before. You must know how to put them back in, too!”

Then again, she thought begrudgingly, the trolls never did recover all her erased memories, which they’d removed when she was a child to protect her from her sister’s magic. To this day, her mind still had holes in it, precious missing moments of time spent with her sister she’d never get back.

Grand Pabbie’s eyes flitted to Kristoff across the valley. “I am sorry, Your Majesty. Our own ways are hard enough to control. Trying to master another’s is almost impossible. I cannot undo what the draugr has done.”

“But that means…Kristoff,” Anna’s voice caught on the name. She thought of the mountain man who had stolen her heart with his love of ice, with the way he spoke on his reindeer’s behalf, with his enthusiastic love of unusual recipes.

Kristoff. Her Kristoff.

Memories flashed through her mind. The first time they’d kissed after she’d presented him with his new sled, the first time they’d played charades. The moment he had gotten down on one knee and asked her to marry him. Kristoff—her Kristoff! Who could now barely remember who she was.

Anna felt her legs buckle. The trolls and Elsa reached for her, but Anna stepped back, unwilling to be helped.

No. She wasn’t willing to accept that Kristoff’s love for her could disappear because of some creature’s doing. And she wasn’t about to let her people suffer from eternal night or never-ending storms, either. She was queen of Arendelle. It was her job to fix this.

Somehow.

Her mind raced, trying to remember Grand Pabbie’s words as he’d consulted with the stars. The troll spoke in riddles. But there was usually a clue buried within them.

What once did flee, now sets sail…

To end this all, you must tell her tale…

Her tale. But they’d told Sissel’s tale! At the campfire. And again in Arendelle…

Suddenly, Anna’s mind flashed back to Oaken’s sauna as they were looking at the portraits of the two princesses. How Oaken had insisted Inger and Sissel were friends, not enemies as Kristoff and the others had claimed. He’d also sworn that Inger had wanted to be a scientist, not a queen like her sister. At the time, Anna had wondered if there could be more to their story.

Now she was convinced there must be.

She turned to Elsa, her face showing her determination.

“The answer is Sissel,” she exclaimed. “We need to figure out exactly what happened between her and Inger. You heard Oaken. He knew things about Inger we didn’t. There’s got to be a piece of the story we’re missing. And maybe whatever it is can help us understand Sissel and what she might want.”

Elsa nodded. “It’s not a bad idea,” she agreed. “But how can we figure out what really happened? Everyone seems to remember it differently. And most of Arendelle doesn’t remember anything at all.”

“True. But it must have been written down at one point,” Anna reminded her. “I mean, it had to be a big story, right? Two princesses visiting Arendelle, and one of them murdering the other? In fact, I bet it was front-page news.”

Her sister’s eyes widened. “Of course! The Village Crown. Their archives go back for years.”

“Maybe we can start there,” Anna said. “I mean, it’s worth a try, right?”

“Absolutely. We should get back to Arendelle as quickly as possible.” Elsa turned to Grand Pabbie. “Thank you for your help,” she said. “We’ll take it from here.”

Grand Pabbie cleared his throat. “Your Majesties, I hope you find what you seek,” he said. “And quickly, too.” He glanced worriedly at Kristoff, who was wandering around aimlessly, happily chatting with rocks that appeared to be actual rocks—not trolls. “In the meantime, why don’t you leave Kristoff with us? We can watch over him until you…resolve…the situation.”

“What? Leave Kristoff?” Anna cried, horrified. Suddenly all her newfound confidence and excitement about solving the mystery seemed to shatter. They wanted her to leave her fiancé behind?

“He’ll be safe from the draugr here,” Elsa reminded her gently.

Anna bowed her head. She knew her sister was right. But still, the thought of leaving him…

“Okay. But you’ll have to keep Sven, too,” she blurted out. “Even if Kristoff doesn’t remember him, those two are never apart.”

Bulda placed a hand on her knee. “Of course! Sven is always welcome here….”

Anna nodded, vacantly, her eyes locking on her fiancé, and her stomach did a somersault all over again. “Just give me a moment to say goodbye. I mean, so long for now,” she corrected herself.

“Of course,” said Elsa, her eyes filled with sympathy. “We’ll give you some space.”

As much as Anna wanted breathing room, she wasn’t looking forward to this farewell. She made her way over to Kristoff and Sven, who were now at least chatting with an actual troll instead of a lifeless rock.

“So you say you’re earning a crystal during this celebration?” Kristoff was saying. “What do these crystals do?”

Little Rock laughed. “Oh, Kristoff!” He saw Anna and smiled. “Hey, your bride is here.” He then bounded off to find the others.

Kristoff did a double take at Anna. “My bride?” His cheeks reddened.

So did hers. “I’m not your bride,” she said quickly. Not yet, anyway, she thought. “But I am someone who cares about you very much.” She touched his cheeks, which were windburned and cold. “That’s why I’m going to leave you and Sven here with Bulda for a few days. Bulda will take good care of you till I get back.”

“Okay,” Kristoff said happily. “And you’re coming back because…?”

Anna felt her heart squeeze so tightly that she lost her breath. But she would be brave. She would not let Kristoff see how scared she was for him and their kingdom. She would make things right. And then she’d never, ever let him tell another campfire story again.

Anna leaned in and kissed him on the lips. “Because I love you,” she said, holding his face close. “And you love me, and we’ve got a whole future to plan when I get back and you start remembering things again.” She stepped away, her heart hurting more than she thought was possible. Her voice was hoarse as she continued, “So stay safe till I do, okay?”

“Okay,” said Kristoff. “Come along, Sven. Let’s go find this Bulda lady.” He paused, then turned to Anna. “Goodbye, Miss Bride!”

Anna ached as she watched him wander through the crowd of trolls without a care in the world. He doesn’t remember us, she thought. He doesn’t remember me. She wanted to cry, but now was when she needed to be strong. So instead, she squared her shoulders and watched from a growing distance as Bulda took his hands and within seconds was talking fast about some terrible-sounding soup that she swore would fix Kristoff and Sven right up.

Anna hoped Bulda was right, but she knew in her heart nothing would bring the love of her life back to her till this draugr business was finished once and for all.

Snow had started falling again as they stopped to pick up Olaf at Oaken’s Trading Post and Sauna and then made their way back into the village later in the day. When they arrived in Arendelle, lights were flickering in every window, but it didn’t appear as if anyone was working on the Polar Nights festivities. In fact, it was as if they didn’t remember the celebration at all.

As they walked toward the newspaper office, they ran into Mattias, who was sitting beneath their parents’ tribute statue, staring down at a photo of himself and Halima, shaking his head, looking puzzled.

“We’re back,” Anna told him. “How has everything been since we were gone?”

Mattias glanced up at the two of them, a blank look on his face. “Everything is fine,” he said flatly. “Why wouldn’t it be?”

Anna’s chest tightened. “Uh, I don’t know. Pirates off our shores? Crazy strong storms? Weird zombies lurking in the shadows?”

“I haven’t heard any of that,” Mattias said with a shrug; Anna’s stomach plummeted. Mattias pushed the photo in his hands in their direction. “Do you happen to know who this is? She looks so familiar, but I can’t place her.”

“Someone special. I think you’ll find her over there,” Elsa said, helping him up from his seat and gently directing him toward Hudson’s Hearth—the tavern owned by the love of his life, whom he currently didn’t seem to remember. Mattias nodded vacantly, then started toward the building. But he seemed to forget where he was going before he was halfway there. Suddenly he began walking in the other direction, whistling tunelessly.

Elsa shot Anna a concerned look. “This isn’t good,” she said. “If Mattias has lost his memories, too, there’s no one to look out for Arendelle.”

“All the more reason we need to get to the bottom of Inger and Sissel’s story fast,” Anna declared, trying not to show how worried she was inside. Her people were counting on her. Kristoff was counting on her—whether he remembered it or not. She couldn’t let any of them down.

And I won’t, she told herself firmly. One way or another, we’re going to stop this draugr. We’re going to make things right.

“Come on,” she said to Elsa. “Let’s go find Wael.”

“Oh, hello!” Wael said as he opened the door to the office of the Village Crown, which he lived above. Anna, Elsa, and Olaf filed in, taking in the smell of ink and warm paper that greeted them. “It’s so nice to have company!”

Anna was startled. The office was a mess, and papers were everywhere. That was not like Wael.

“‘Nice to have company’? This is new,” Olaf mumbled. Wael was usually too busy to talk unless he was doing an interview, and when he was working, he was super serious.

“Wael, we were actually hoping to ask you some questions about the paper,” Anna started right in.

Wael’s face fell. “I’m afraid there is no new issue this week. I seem to have forgotten how to work my printing press…and I can’t find my ink. Have you seen my pencil anywhere?”

Elsa reached up and pulled it out from where it was tucked behind Wael’s ear.

“Oh!” Wael chuckled. “Silly me! So forgetful today.”

Anna glanced at her sister. “That’s what we were afraid of.” It appeared, like everyone else, Wael would be no help. Any research would have to be done on their own.

“Wael,” Elsa addressed him. “We’re hoping to look at your archives. Where do you keep all the old issues of the paper?”

Wael brightened. “In the back room! I have all of them, dating back to the paper’s first issue.” He hurried ahead of them, dodging stacks of this week’s forgotten issue. “The Village Crown has been around for…uh…”

“Sixty years,” Olaf offered.

“Right!” Wael said, smiling again. “Nice to meet fans of our work.” He opened the door to the back room, and Anna saw walls of bookshelves with papers stacked on them. “Take your time and look at anything you want,” Wael said. “I’ll be in the other room, um…working on something.” He chuckled to himself and disappeared.

“Well,” Elsa said as she went to the first bookshelf. “At least a forgetful Wael is a friendly Wael.”

“Okay, let’s divide and conquer,” Anna said, heading to the second bookshelf. “We’re looking for a story that ran about fifty years ago.”

“That narrows it down,” said Olaf, hopping up on a stool and tackling the third bookcase.

The search took a while, Anna’s patience wearing thin as Wael whistled happily in the next room. Before long, the place looked like a hurricane had hit it, with stacks of papers now piled in disarray high on either side of them and scattered all over the floor. (Turned out, Olaf’s version of researching was a bit…messy.) They’d found all sorts of interesting stories from years past: their parents’ wedding announcement, the grand opening of Blodget’s Bakery, the tragic story of Queen Rita—King Runeard’s wife and their grandmother—and her strange disappearance when their father was just a small child. But nothing about the Vesterland sisters.

“Ooh, here’s a story about your birth, Anna!” Olaf announced excitedly, pushing a crumpled paper in her direction. Anna scanned the front page, then frowned.

“Uh, where?” she asked, confused.

“It’s right there!” Olaf pointed to the bottom of the page. “Right under that really big article about ‘Old Blue Eyes’ the Pirate Queen threatening Arendelle’s shores!”

“Of course it is,” Anna grumbled, her eyes falling to the much smaller headline, ARENDELLE WELCOMES THEIR SECOND PRINCESS! Clearly the Village Crown’s obsession with pirates ran deep….

“I think I found something!” Elsa shouted, jumping down from a top shelf with several papers in her arms. She dropped them on the table and pointed to the paper on top. “It’s an article about the Vesterland sisters visiting Arendelle. And the timing is right.” She laid out the newspaper on the table. Sure enough, there was a drawing of two girls—one with long hair tied up in complicated braids and one with a short bob—staring back at them. Elsa touched the newspaper. “That’s them. The same girls in Oaken’s portrait.” She pointed to the long-haired girl. “Inger,” she said, then moved her hand to the girl with the bob. “And Sissel.”

“I have to say, Sissel’s a lot prettier as a real girl than a rotting zombie,” Olaf observed. “I mean, not that looks matter. It’s what’s in your heart that counts.”

Anna stared at the picture of Sissel. It was hard to believe the creature that had attacked them had once been this beautiful girl. She looked so happy, as if she hadn’t had a care in the world. But then, so did Inger, who was smiling adoringly up at her sister in the picture, like she worshipped the ground Sissel walked on. One thing was for sure: they definitely didn’t look like mortal enemies.

Elsa started reading the story aloud. “‘The Village Crown is pleased to report that the princesses of Vesterland, known as the Vesterland sisters, are coming to Arendelle for an important meeting with King Runeard.’”

Anna frowned. “An important meeting? About what?”

“It doesn’t say,” Elsa told her, flipping ahead to another story. “Here’s one about the accident, though.” The three of them leaned over the paper and read the article at the same time.

“It’s just like everyone in the village has already been saying,” Anna said, knowing she sounded disappointed. “Inger and Sissel had an argument, and Sissel drowned. Inger was charged with her murder, and Grandfather had her sent away on a prison ship to be banished. It went down at sea in a storm before it made it to its destination. There’s nothing else to report.”

“If Inger is dead, then what could Sissel be after by appearing now?” Elsa asked. “Not revenge, clearly.”

“I don’t know. But this isn’t telling us anything new.” She put the paper back down. “We need to find out more about the sisters themselves. Or what they were arguing about that was so bad it led to murder.”

“Well, we won’t find that here,” Elsa said.

Anna nodded slowly, feeling discouraged. “And clearly no one in Arendelle remembers anything,” she began. Then a thought came to her. “That’s it! Why didn’t I think of this before?”

“What?” Elsa asked, looking puzzled.

“We need to go to Vesterland!” Anna said, getting excited. “Maybe King Jonas and Mari know why Inger and Sissel were here in Arendelle or what they were arguing about. I mean, that’s their home kingdom! If anyone would know, it would be them!”

“Great idea, Anna,” Elsa agreed. “A visit to King Jonas could solve all our problems.”

Anna smiled dreamily as she closed the book. Solve all our problems. Get Kristoff back. She suddenly felt hopeful. “Let’s inform Mattias and leave first thing in the morning.”
