sentences.zh: 正如她们如今所知，祖父规划的这座水坝最终对环境造成了灾难性后果，切断了北地人的水源，使他们土地干涸。

sentences.en: It was only recently, after Anna finally destroyed the dam with the help of the Earth Giants, that the land had begun to recover and things had gotten back to normal.
sentences.zh: 直到最近，在安娜借助大地巨人之力终于摧毁水坝后，那片土地才开始恢复，一切才回归正常。

sentences.en: King Jonas scratched his beard. “I can’t say for certain, but if she wasn’t, I couldn’t imagine her standing up to King Runeard about it.
sentences.zh: 乔纳斯国王挠了挠胡子。“我说不准，但如果她不赞成，我也难以想象她会为此去顶撞鲁尼尔德国王。

sentences.en: From what I understand, she was pretty shy.
sentences.zh: 据我所知，她相当害羞。

sentences.en: It was her sister, Inger, who was the fighter in the family.” He seemed to consider this for a moment. “Hmm.
sentences.zh: 家里那个爱抗争的是她妹妹英格。”他似乎琢磨了一会儿。“嗯。

sentences.en: Maybe that’s why she took Inger along with her on that trip to Arendelle?” “Speaking of fighting, do you know if they got along?” Anna pressed. “Some say they were rivals and others say they loved each other.
sentences.zh: 也许正因为这样，她才在那次去阿伦黛尔时带上了英格？”“说到争执，你知道她们相处得好吗？”安娜追问。“有人说她们是对手，也有人说她们相亲相爱。

sentences.en: It’s hard to get a straight story.” King Jonas chuckled and looked at Mari. “Sounds like typical siblings to me.
sentences.zh: 很难听到一个确切的说法。”乔纳斯国王轻笑，看着玛丽。“依我看，这就像典型的兄弟姐妹。

sentences.en: Don’t all brothers and sisters get along sometimes and fight like dogs at others?” Anna and Elsa looked at one another and mumbled some variation of “yes.” King Jonas snapped his fingers. “You know who you should talk to about them?
sentences.zh: 哪对兄弟姐妹不是时而和睦、时而打得不可开交？”安娜和艾莎对视一眼，含糊地应了声“是啊”。乔纳斯国王打了个响指。“你们知道该找谁打听她们的事吗？

sentences.en: The Figels.
sentences.zh: 菲格勒夫妇。

sentences.en: They were their castle stewards who looked after them.
sentences.zh: 他们是照顾她们的城堡管家。

sentences.en: They’re retired now, but they practically raised the girls when they were younger.” “The Figels!
sentences.zh: 如今退休了，但姑娘们小时候基本是他们带大的。”“菲格勒夫妇！

sentences.en: Yes!
sentences.zh: 对！

sentences.en: We’d love to talk to them,” Anna said, excitement welling inside of her.
sentences.zh: 我们很想和他们谈谈，”安娜说，内心涌起一阵兴奋。

sentences.en: This was exactly what they needed: people who had actually known the sisters personally. “I can take you to them,” Mari said. “They live right in the village.
sentences.zh: 这正是她们需要的：真正认识姐妹俩的人。“我带你们去，”玛丽说。“他们就住在村里。

sentences.en: You’ll love them!” She paused, then grinned. “Just…don’t eat anything they try to serve you.
sentences.zh: 你们会喜欢他们的！”她顿了顿，咧嘴一笑。“只是……别吃他们端给你的任何东西。

sentences.en: Trust me, you’ll thank me later.” The Figels’ modest home was literally right outside the castle gates.
sentences.zh: 相信我，以后你会谢我的。”菲格勒夫妇简朴的家就在城堡大门外。

sentences.en: Even better: someone answered on the first knock.
sentences.zh: 更妙的是：第一声敲门就有人应了。

sentences.en: The strong smell of garlic, onions, and cooked fish met them at the door. “Oh my,” Elsa whispered, inhaling sharply. “Hello there, Mari!” said a tall woman with salt-and-pepper hair.
sentences.zh: 一开门，浓烈的蒜、洋葱和炖鱼味扑面而来。“哎呀，”艾莎倒吸一口气，低声说。“你好啊，玛丽！”一位花白头发的高个女人说。

sentences.en: She was dressed in a bright orange apron that covered an even brighter blue dress. “You’re just in time!
sentences.zh: 她穿着亮橙色的围裙，底下是更鲜亮的蓝裙子。“你来得太巧了！

sentences.en: Olga and I were just trying out a new stew recipe.” Mari looked at Anna out of the corner of her eye. “Oh…I couldn’t impose.
sentences.zh: 我和奥尔加刚在试一道新炖菜谱。”玛丽用眼角余光瞥了安娜一下。“哦……我们不好打扰。

sentences.en: I just wanted to stop by to introduce you to my friends.” “Nonsense!” said the woman, smiling at Anna. “We love company!
sentences.zh: 我只是顺路过来，把朋友们介绍给你。”“哪儿的话！”那女人对安娜笑着说。“我们最喜欢有人来做客了！

sentences.en: I’m Helga.
sentences.zh: 我是赫尔加。

sentences.en: I’ll tell my wife to set three more plates.” She grabbed Mari’s hand and yanked her inside. “OLGA!
sentences.zh: 我去叫妻子再加三个盘子。”她抓住玛丽的手把她拽进屋。“奥尔加！

sentences.en: MARI IS HERE!” The home was dark with the curtains drawn, but tidy, with lots of knits and piles of socks everywhere.
sentences.zh: 玛丽来了！”屋里拉着窗帘，光线昏暗，但很整洁，到处是针织物和一摞摞袜子。

sentences.en: The smell of food was even stronger inside the house.
sentences.zh: 屋里的食物气味更浓了。

sentences.en: Anna’s eyes started to water. “That’s so kind of you, but we actually just ate.” Her stomach grumbled in response.
sentences.zh: 安娜的眼睛开始泛泪。“你们太好心了，不过我们其实刚吃过。”她的肚子却不争气地叫了起来。

sentences.en: Helga laughed. “Looks like you’ve got room,” she said, pulling out a chair for Anna.
sentences.zh: 赫尔加笑了。“看来你还有肚子，”她说着给安娜拉出一把椅子。

sentences.en: Elsa and Mari grabbed their own. “OLGA!
sentences.zh: 艾莎和玛丽各自拉了把椅子。“奥尔加！

sentences.en: EXTRA PLATES!
sentences.zh: 再加几个盘子！

sentences.en: She’s a little hard of hearing these days,” Helga told the group. “I’m coming!
sentences.zh: 她如今有点耳背，”赫尔加对大家说。“来啦！

sentences.en: I’m coming!” Olga came around the corner balancing three plates of steaming hot food in her arms.
sentences.zh: 来啦！”奥尔加从角落转出来，怀里稳稳端着三盘热气腾腾的食物。

sentences.en: Her white hair was pulled up into a messy bun, and she was wearing a similar orange apron, which was splattered with all kinds of food.
sentences.zh: 她白发挽成凌乱的发髻，穿着类似的橙色围裙，上面溅着各种食物渍。

sentences.en: She saw the company waiting and smiled. “Hello, dears!
sentences.zh: 她看见客人们在等，笑了。“你们好啊，亲爱的！

sentences.en: What a nice surprise.
sentences.zh: 真是个惊喜。

sentences.en: So glad you can stay for lunch.” She plunked down plates in front of the girls, and Anna could have sworn she smelled cloudberries in the dark brown soup.
sentences.zh: 真高兴你们能留下来吃午饭。”她把盘子啪地放在姑娘们面前，安娜发誓在那深棕色的汤里闻到了云莓味。

sentences.en: She picked up her spoon warily. “Oh…how…nice.
sentences.zh: 她警惕地拿起勺子。“哦……真……不错。

sentences.en: What is this?” “ Lapskaus ,” Helga told them. “We didn’t have all the ingredients for Olga’s mom’s recipe, so we just winged it.” “We do that a lot,” Olga told Anna. “We use whatever we have on hand, and it usually turns out okay.” “Usually,” Helga seconded. “You should stay for dessert.
sentences.zh: 这是什么？”“拉普斯考斯（杂烩炖菜），”赫尔加告诉他们。“我们凑不齐奥尔加妈妈配方里的材料，就随便发挥了。”“我们常这么干，”奥尔加对安娜说。“手边有什么就用什么，通常还行。”“通常吧，”赫尔加附和。“你们该留下来吃甜点。

sentences.en: We’re making tilslørte bondepiker .
sentences.zh: 我们在做提尔什勒特·邦德皮克（苹果甜点）。

sentences.en: It’s delicious if you like apples.” “We’re out of apples,” Olga reminded her. “But we could try making it with onions!
sentences.zh: 喜欢苹果的话很好吃。”“我们没苹果了，”奥尔加提醒她。“不过我们可以试试用洋葱做！

sentences.en: We have extra.” “Ooh, good idea!” Helga clapped her hands.
sentences.zh: 我们还有多的。”“噢，好主意！”赫尔加拍起手来。

sentences.en: Anna’s stomach turned at the thought of an onion-centric dessert. “We don’t want to keep you from baking,” Anna said quickly. “We were just hoping to talk to you about the Vesterland sisters.
sentences.zh: 想到以洋葱为主角的甜点，安娜的胃一阵翻腾。“我们不想耽误你们烘焙，”安娜赶紧说。“我们只是想和你们聊聊维斯特兰姐妹。

sentences.en: Mari mentioned you were their stewards.” “These are my friends, Anna and Elsa, the queens of Arendelle,” Mari explained. “I told them you knew the girls well.” Helga’s eyes lit up. “Oh!
sentences.zh: 玛丽说你们曾是她们的管家。”“这两位是我的朋友，安娜和艾莎，阿伦黛尔的女王，”玛丽解释。“我跟他们说你们很了解那两个姑娘。”赫尔加眼睛一亮。“哦！

sentences.en: We haven’t talked about them in a long time.” Olga hurried back into the room with two more plates for her and Helga. “We looked after them after their parents were gone, and we grew very close.” “I can imagine,” Anna said softly. “Elsa and I are really close with our castle stewards, too.” She thought of Kai and Gerda and her heart lurched.
sentences.zh: 我们很久没聊她们了。”奥尔加又端着两个盘子匆匆回屋，给自己和赫尔加的。“她们父母走后是我们照顾她们，我们变得很亲近。”“我能想象，”安娜轻声说。“艾莎和我跟我们的城堡管家也很亲。”她想起凯和格尔达，心头一紧。

sentences.en: At the moment, they couldn’t even remember who the girls were. “That’s lovely,” Helga said. “We loved working for the family.
sentences.zh: 此刻，他们连这两个姑娘是谁都记不起来了。“那真好，”赫尔加说。“我们很喜欢为这家工作。

sentences.en: Inger and Sissel were two peas in a pod, tighter than two sisters ever could be.” Olga’s eyes locked on Anna.
sentences.zh: 英格和希塞尔形影不离，比任何两姐妹都更要好。”奥尔加的目光锁定在安娜身上。

sentences.en: Her jaw dropped. “That locket you’re wearing!” Her eyes narrowed suspiciously. “Where did you get that?” “Um, it’s a long story,” Anna stammered. “You recognize the locket?” Elsa pressed curiously. “Recognize it!
sentences.zh: 她惊得张大了嘴。“你戴的那个小盒！”她眯起眼，狐疑地打量。“你从哪儿弄来的？”“呃，说来话长，”安娜结巴道。“你认得这个小盒？”艾莎好奇地追问。“认得！

sentences.en: Of course I recognize it!
sentences.zh: 我当然认得！

sentences.en: I gave those lockets to the girls the year their parents died.
sentences.zh: 那年她们父母去世，是我把那些小盒送给姑娘们的。

sentences.en: So they’d remember they weren’t alone.
sentences.zh: 好让她们记得自己并不孤单。

sentences.en: They’d always have each other.” Olga sank into the chair, her eyes misting. “Inger lost hers immediately, of course.
sentences.zh: 她们永远有彼此。”奥尔加跌坐进椅子，眼眶湿润。“英格当然立刻就把自己的弄丢了。

sentences.en: Silly girl.
sentences.zh: 傻丫头。

sentences.en: But she always got away with mishaps like that—she had these bright blue eyes that were—” “Magnetic!” Helga finished. “Such an extraordinary color.
sentences.zh: 不过她这种小差错总能蒙混过去——她有一双明亮的蓝眼睛，简直——”“摄人心魄！”赫尔加接话。“那样非凡的颜色。

sentences.en: And Sissel…she was always so into her appearance.
sentences.zh: 而希塞尔……她总是特别在意外表。

sentences.en: She never took her necklace off.
sentences.zh: 她从不摘下项链。

sentences.en: She told me it was her favorite piece of jewelry—and let me tell you, those two girls had their options when it came to jewels.” She hobbled up to Anna, palming the locket and popping it open.
sentences.zh: 她告诉我那是她最爱的首饰——跟你说，那两个姑娘在珠宝上可挑得很。”她蹒跚走到安娜跟前，托起小盒把它打开。

sentences.en: She beckoned her wife to come over, all talk of stew thankfully forgotten. “That’s our girls,” Helga said sadly. “I mean, they weren’t ours, but they…” “They felt like family,” Olga finished. “Inger always acted like the older one—a tad bossy, as I told her, with Sissel as quiet as a mouse.
sentences.zh: 她招呼妻子过来，幸好关于炖菜的话题被抛到了脑后。“那就是我们的姑娘，”赫尔加伤心地说。“我是说，她们不是我们的，但她们……”“就像家人一样，”奥尔加接上。“英格总像姐姐——有点爱发号施令，我跟她说过，而希塞尔安静得像只老鼠。

sentences.en: But”—Olga shrugged—“Sissel was older, and it was her duty to take the throne, so Inger helped her best she could.” Anna snuck a glance at Elsa.
sentences.zh: 但”——奥尔加耸耸肩——“希塞尔年长，继承王位是她的责任，所以英格尽所能帮她。”安娜偷偷瞥了艾莎一眼。

sentences.en: Some of the similarities really were uncanny, personality-wise. “Do you remember Inger ever talking about wanting to be queen?” Elsa asked.
sentences.zh: 有些相似之处的确诡异地契合，单论性格。“你记得英格有没有说过想当女王？”艾莎问。

sentences.en: Helga stirred a spoon in the stew in front of her. “I don’t know about that.
sentences.zh: 赫尔加搅了搅面前的炖菜。“那我说不好。

sentences.en: Inger was a naturalist—very concerned with the cutting down of trees and polluting water.
sentences.zh: 英格是个自然主义者——非常在意砍伐树木和污染水源的事。

sentences.en: She cared a lot about preserving Vesterland’s waters, wildlife, and nature.
sentences.zh: 她很关心保护维斯特兰的水域、野生动植物和自然。

sentences.en: Sissel, however, was more concerned with protecting alliances.
sentences.zh: 而希塞尔更关心维护同盟关系。

sentences.en: She was a woman of the people.” That’s what Oaken had said.
sentences.zh: 她是个亲民的人。”奥肯也是这么说的。

sentences.en: Anna glanced at Elsa.
sentences.zh: 安娜瞥了艾莎一眼。

sentences.en: A picture of the girls was becoming clearer. “Hmm.
sentences.zh: 两个姑娘的画像渐渐清晰起来。“嗯。

sentences.en: Sounds like they might have been divided on the dam project, then.
sentences.zh: 看来她们在那座水坝工程上可能立场分歧。

sentences.en: I mean, if Inger realized its impact on the environment…” Elsa’s eyes widened in realization. “Do you think that’s what they were fighting about, then?
sentences.zh: 我是说，如果英格意识到了它对环境的破坏……”艾莎恍然大悟，睁大眼睛。“那你觉得，她们争执的是这个吗？

sentences.en: The dam project?
sentences.zh: 那座水坝工程？

sentences.en: I mean, it happened in Arendelle, right after they met with King Runeard.” Anna pursed her lips. “Maybe…but a fight that led to murder?” She looked up at Olga and Helga.
sentences.zh: 我是说，事情就发生在阿伦黛尔，就在她们见过鲁尼尔德国王之后。”安娜抿起嘴唇。“也许……可一场争执会演变成谋杀？”她抬头看向奥尔加和赫尔加。

sentences.en: It was time to just acknowledge the elephant in the room. “Do you think Inger murdered Sissel?” Olga dropped her spoon in her stew. “Definitely not.
sentences.zh: 是时候直面那个房间里的大象了。“你们觉得英格谋杀了希塞尔吗？”奥尔加的勺子掉进炖菜里。“绝对没有。

sentences.en: I know what people say about the matter, but I can’t believe it.
sentences.zh: 我知道外界怎么传，可我不信。

sentences.en: I won’t!
sentences.zh: 我不信！

sentences.en: Having known Inger, she would never…” She trailed off, unable to go on.
sentences.zh: 我了解英格，她绝不会……”她哽咽着说不下去了。

sentences.en: Helga put her arm around her, producing a handkerchief from her pocket and giving it to her.
sentences.zh: 赫尔加搂住她，从口袋里掏出手帕递给她。

sentences.en: Olga blew her nose loudly. “We don’t mean to bring up such a sad memory,” Elsa said quietly. “We’re just trying to figure out what really happened that day.
sentences.zh: 奥尔加大声擤了擤鼻子。“我们不是故意勾起这么伤心的回忆，”艾莎轻声说。“我们只是想弄清那天到底发生了什么。

sentences.en: If there’s more to the story.” Helga nodded. “We’ve long wondered, too, but we’ve made our peace with it.
sentences.zh: 如果事情另有隐情的话。”赫尔加点点头。“我们也疑惑了很久，但已经释怀了。

sentences.en: We just try to remember the girls the way they were.” Anna’s shoulders drooped.
sentences.zh: 我们只是尽量记得姑娘们本来的样子。”安娜垂下肩膀。

sentences.en: Another dead end. “And honor their memory as best we can,” Olga added, sighing deeply. “By bringing people to visit the memorial we built them in Arendelle.” Anna stopped twirling her spoon. “Memorial?
sentences.zh: 又是一条死路。“并尽我们所能纪念她们，”奥尔加深叹一口气补充。“就是带人去参观我们在阿伦黛尔为她们建的纪念碑。”安娜停下转动勺子的手。“纪念碑？

sentences.en: What memorial?” “After the incident, we traveled to Arendelle to try to find out what we could.
sentences.zh: 什么纪念碑？”“那件事发生后，我们去了阿伦黛尔，想尽量弄清情况。

sentences.en: We had someone take us to the spot where it happened—where Sissel…” Helga choked up. “We made a small memorial to both girls.
sentences.zh: 我们让人带我们去了事发地点——希塞尔……”赫尔加哽咽了。“我们为两个姑娘建了一座小纪念碑。

sentences.en: Over the years it has been visited by many who loved them as we did.” Olga smiled proudly at her wife. “Helga carved a wooden statue of the girls that we brought there in our wagon.
sentences.zh: 这些年来，许多像我们一样爱她们的人来凭吊过。”奥尔加自豪地对妻子笑了笑。“赫尔加雕刻了一座姑娘们的木像，我们用马车运到了那里。

sentences.en: We planted wildflowers around it.
sentences.zh: 我们在四周种了野花。

sentences.en: They were Sissel’s favorite.” Anna’s heart started beating with excitement.
sentences.zh: 那是希塞尔最喜欢的花。”安娜的心兴奋地跳动起来。

sentences.en: A memorial.
sentences.zh: 一座纪念碑。

sentences.en: But more importantly, a memorial set up in the exact spot Sissel drowned.
sentences.zh: 但更重要的是，这座纪念碑就立在希塞尔溺亡的确切地点。

sentences.en: If they could get there, perhaps Elsa could use her powers to pull up a memory.
sentences.zh: 如果能到那里，也许艾莎能用她的魔力唤起一段记忆。

sentences.en: And they could learn what had truly happened on that day.
sentences.zh: 她们就能弄清那一天究竟发生了什么。

sentences.en: This might prove to be their best lead yet. “How would we find this memorial?” Elsa asked, her voice catching.
sentences.zh: 这或许是他们迄今最好的线索。“我们要怎么找到这座纪念碑？”艾莎问，声音有些发紧。

sentences.en: Her sister clearly had the same thoughts she did. “We’ll give you a map,” Olga said. “We made them to share with others who wanted to make the pilgrimage to pay their respects.
sentences.zh: 她姐姐显然和我想到一块儿了。“我们给你地图，”奥尔加说。“我们制作了一些，分发给想来朝圣凭吊的人。

sentences.en: HELGA!
sentences.zh: 赫尔加！

sentences.en: Give the girls a map!” “Stop yelling!” Helga chided her. “I’m not yelling,” Olga insisted and looked at Anna. “She’s a bit hard of hearing.” Helga went to a curio cabinet and pulled open a bottom drawer, then produced a piece of parchment, which she handed to Elsa.
sentences.zh: 给姑娘们一张地图！”“别喊了！”赫尔加训她。“我没喊，”奥尔加坚持道，又看着安娜。“她有点耳背。”赫尔加走到一个陈列柜前拉开底层抽屉，取出一张羊皮纸，递给艾莎。

sentences.en: On it was a drawing of Arendelle’s rivers with an X next to one near the village.
sentences.zh: 上面画着阿伦黛尔的河流，村落附近的一条河边标了个叉。

chapters.title: Chapter Fifteen: Elsa
chapters.en:
HELGA’S MAP, it turned out, wasn’t exactly pinpoint accurate. In fact, they got lost in the dark woods three times before finally stumbling their way to the small, crude wooden statue honoring the two Vesterland princesses plopped down on a stone pedestal at a bend in the river. Elsa pointed to it with a cheer and Anna let out a sigh of relief, dropping off Havski and rushing over to it. She placed her hands on her hips, examining the carved wood.

“You know, maybe Sissel just wants a new memorial,” she remarked, poking at the spot where Sissel’s arm should have been. It had clearly broken off at some point over the years, and some of the wood was rotted clear through. “I mean, this one’s kind of falling apart.”

“Imagine if it were that simple.” Elsa smiled as she slipped off the Water Nokk and stepped up to Anna. She squinted at the wooden memorial, which had clearly seen better days. She supposed fifty years of exposure to the elements would do that to any piece of wood. Still, the lettering at the bottom was clear enough to read.

BELOVED PRINCESSES. MAY YOU REST IN PEACE.

Hopefully they could make that happen—and soon, too.

“This is definitely the same spot I saw in my vision,” Elsa mused, her eyes rising to the rapidly flowing water. “I remember that boulder just offshore. And that tree is much larger now, but it was definitely there,” she added, pointing to a large oak with branches that hung over the river. She nodded. “Yes, this is definitely the spot where Sissel drowned.”

“But did Inger do it?” Anna asked. “That’s the question we need answered. And if she did—why? Everything we’ve learned about the sisters so far makes it seem like they were close. That they loved each other.”

“Right. I mean, sure, they disagreed on a few things, but so what?” Elsa asked. “I mean, we disagree all the time.”

“Usually about you putting yourself in danger,” Anna pointed out.

Elsa snorted. She turned back to the memorial. “In my Ahtohallan vision, I saw Sissel struggling in the water. But we need to go back further. To hear what they were fighting about and what happened. That’s the only way to know for sure.”

She turned to the river. It was rushing past them pretty hard, tossing around large chunks of ice in the current. Very unlike the slow, serene section they were familiar with that ran by Arendelle’s town center. Elsa guessed there might be a glacier nearby, feeding the river with melted snow. Even a good swimmer would have a tough time keeping their head above water there.

She dropped her hand into the river and felt the current through her fingers.

“Do you sense anything?” Anna asked eagerly. Elsa shook her head.

“Just freezing cold water,” she replied, frowning. She closed her eyes, thinking of Sissel and Inger. Trying to imagine them on this shore. Arguing. What were they arguing about?

But nothing came to her.

It was then that she realized the problem. Water had memory. But this particular current wasn’t the same water that had been here when Sissel had drowned. River water was constantly moving, always changing. If Elsa were in Ahtohallan, maybe she could manage to pull something up with the help of the spirit of memories. But here—she was on her own, and she wasn’t sure it was going to work.

Elsa slumped onto the riverbank, feeling discouraged. What good were her powers if she couldn’t use them to help anyone? Had this all been a dead end? Frustration began to rise inside of her. She squeezed her hands into fists.

“Hey! Elsa! Relax.” She felt Anna by her side, putting her arms around her. “It’s okay.”

“It’s not okay!” Elsa snapped. “I need to figure this out!” She squirmed free of Anna’s grasp and dunked her hands in the freezing cold water again. Maybe if she could go deeper, she could find something. She squeezed her eyes shut. Trying, trying.

SPLASH!

Elsa screamed as she lost her balance, tumbling headfirst into the icy river. She thrashed around, trying to lodge her feet against the slippery stones, while choking on a mouthful of dirty water. The current was strong, dragging her downstream fast.

“Anna!” she cried, trying to use her magic to freeze the rushing water. But nothing happened. It was as if she were wearing gloves, even though she wasn’t. She’d probably drained her powers reaching so deep, and now they were fizzling out again.

Oh, no. No, no, no!

“Anna! Help!” she cried again, knowing she sounded scared. Desperate. She fought to keep her head above water, to suck in air in the moments she could. But instead, she was gulping river water too fast, choking and sputtering as she tried again to find the river’s bottom. But it was deep here and her feet only kicked uselessly as the current dragged her further down. Her body began to weaken. The riverbank seemed miles away.

“Elsa! I’ve got you!”

Suddenly, she felt strong arms grab her, dragging her to the shore. Anna heaved her onto dry land, then rolled her over, slapping her hard on the back until she hacked up all the dirty water. Elsa’s heart pumped madly in her chest as she sucked in breath after breath of clean air.

“Are you okay?” Anna’s voice sounded very concerned. “Elsa! Talk to me!”

She struggled to sit up. “I think so.” She swallowed hard, trying to stop her body from shaking in a mixture of terror and cold. “I just leaned in too far.”

“Yeah, I saw.” Anna pursed her lips together. “You scared me half to death. I thought…” She trailed off, unable to continue. But Elsa knew exactly what she’d been thinking. That she’d almost shared Sissel’s fate.

Elsa wrung out her white dress, staring at the river ruefully. “I guess now I understand how Sissel drowned,” she said. “That current is rough.”

“Lucky for you, you have a strong sister.” Anna gathered up a small pile of wood and leaves. “Bruni?” she called out to the Fire Spirit when she was finished. “Want to help warm up your girl?”

The spirit leapt onto the small pile, easily igniting it with its flames. Soon they had a small fire giving off a nice hot glow. Elsa sighed gratefully, warming her hands. Her heart, however, was still beating very fast.

“So much for that plan,” she said sorrowfully, giving the river an annoyed look. She hugged her chest. “Sorry I dragged you all the way out here,” she said. “It was probably a dumb idea. I just thought…I mean, I remember pulling the memory from our parents’ ship. But that water had been there for years—so the memories were still there, inside of it. This water is all new. There’s nothing to pull from it. I’m sorry, Anna. I really wanted to figure out Sissel’s story so we could end this.” Her voice broke.

“Water has memory,” Anna whispered thoughtfully.

“Yes. I just said that. But—”

“But the water here isn’t the same. You need something that might have remnants of water from back then, right?”

“Right. But that’s impossible. It was fifty years ago.”

“Maybe not.”

Elsa cocked her head in question. Anna lifted Sissel’s locket from around her neck and held it out to her sister.

“Remember how the portraits seemed warped?” she said. “Like they’d been underwater? Maybe they still have a bit of it in them.”

“Anna! You’re a genius!” Elsa plucked the locket from her sister’s fingers, palming it in her hands. “The Figels told us Sissel never went anywhere without her locket. Which meant she must have been wearing it when she drowned.” Her breath caught in her throat as hope surged through her. She tried to tell herself not to get too excited, but she couldn’t help it.

She wrapped her fingers around the locket. Then she closed her eyes, searching deep for her powers. For a moment, she felt nothing and worried they had fizzled again. But then, slowly, the familiar feeling began to rise inside of her.

“It’s working! Elsa, it’s working!”

Elsa’s eyes flew open. Sure enough, a small mist seemed to be rising from her closed hand. She released her fingers, opening them up one by one. The mist was twining out from the locket.

And suddenly they could see it perfectly. Two girls. One with long hair tied up in complicated braids. The other with a short bob.

“Inger and Sissel,” Elsa breathed. Anna looked as mesmerized as she felt. Even more so when the voices began to rise in the air.

“Inger, you need to stop arguing with him! It’s not going to work.”

“But, Sissel, we have to try! He’s already started clearing land. If he builds that dam, it’s going to destroy the Enchanted Forest and all the Northuldra’s territory. It’ll be an environmental disaster.”

Elsa gasped. So they had been fighting about the dam that day! And Inger definitely wasn’t in favor of it.

“Look, I understand. I really do,” Sissel broke in. “But what are we going to do? King Runeard is never going to listen to us. And if we try to fight him on this, he’s going to punish Vesterland. Our actual people. I mean, I care about reindeer and bunnies and all that, too, but I also care about our citizens. As their future queen, I need to protect them. Arendelle controls the port—all the food and supplies and medicine coming in from other kingdoms. Without that, we will suffer greatly.”

“We will also suffer if all the animals die or migrate further north,” Inger argued. “What are we going to hunt for food? He has to know the greater impacts his dam will have on our lands.”

Sissel sighed. “He already knows. He just doesn’t care.”

“You have to make him care! That’s what a queen would do!”

The sisters stared at one another, clearly at a standoff. Elsa glanced over at Anna, who was watching the scene with horrified eyes.

“Yeah, well, maybe you should be queen, then!” Sissel shot back. “If you’re such an expert and all!”

“You know I don’t want that,” Inger protested, sounding hurt. “And you know I think you’ll be an amazing queen. You’re already an amazing sister. I’m just trying to help. Don’t shut me out. Please!”

For a moment, Sissel just bristled. Then her shoulders began to slump. She sighed deeply, then gave her sister an apologetic look. “I’m sorry. I didn’t mean that. I love you; you know that.”

“And I love you.” Inger reached for Sissel’s hand. “We’ll figure this out. One way or another.”

Elsa watched, entranced, as the two sisters embraced on the side of the river. No longer fighting with one another, just hugging each other tightly. Just like she and Anna did after they argued.

“So it’s true. Inger didn’t want to be queen. She was just trying to help Sissel,” Anna whispered, also looking on in awe. “She loved her sister.”

“Then what happened between them that could have led to Sissel’s death?” Elsa asked. “I don’t get it.”

“Just keep watching!” Anna urged. “There’s got to be more.”

But the vision was already fading. The magic drained from her fingers. Elsa gritted her teeth, trying to keep it going, but she could feel it falling away. The mist began to sputter from the necklace. The vision began to dim. She squeezed her eyes shut, straining. Feeling the ice crackle on her skin. No! After all this, she couldn’t lose it now. She just couldn’t!

“Elsa, look!”

Elsa’s eyes shot open. Her mouth gaped, realizing they were no longer alone. Standing by the memorial statue, seeming to have come out of nowhere, was the draugr itself. Where had it come from? Had it followed them here?

This was not good. Not good at all.

“Anna, back away slowly. Don’t make any sudden moves. I’ll distract it and then find you later,” Elsa whispered to her sister, her mind racing with a plan. Ice hadn’t stopped the draugr last time. But maybe it could slow the creature down enough for them to get away.

She glanced at Anna, who hadn’t moved. “What are you waiting for?” she cried, fear pounding in her heart. “Go!”

But Anna didn’t go. Instead, she stepped between her sister and the draugr.

“What are you doing?” Elsa choked out, horrified. Her eyes locked onto the draugr, waiting for it to strike. Anna was too close. Far too close. It would only take one swipe of the creature’s claws, and…“Anna, it’s going to attack you!”

Or worse…

“No,” Anna said firmly, keeping her eyes glued to it. “I think if it was, it would have done it already. I think it wants us here. I think it has something to show us. The draugr was the one who left us the locket,” she reminded Elsa. “Maybe it hoped you could pull something from it. In fact, maybe that’s why it’s been haunting us all along. Because you’re the only one with the power to see into the past. To discover the true story behind the sisters.”

“Sissssster…” the creature moaned, its eyes seemingly aflame when saying the word. “Sisssssster. Minnnnne.”

The draugr raised a rotted finger, pointing it toward the locket in Elsa’s hand. For a moment, nothing happened. Then, suddenly, the sputtering stream of mist began to thicken, get stronger.

“Yes!” Anna cried out in excitement. “Yes!”

Elsa watched in amazement as more mist began to spill from the necklace, onto the riverbank, rebuilding the vision they’d been watching before. Slowly, with their combined magic, the vision grew more solid, real. As if the two girls were standing right in front of them.

“Now, let’s see what really happened that day,” Anna declared, her voice high-pitched with excitement.

Biting her lower lip, Elsa turned back to the scene playing out in front of them, concentrating hard to keep the magic flowing. Inger and Sissel were stepping out of their embrace, smiling at each other.

“I’m sorry,” Inger said. “I don’t want to fight with you.”

“No, I’m sorry!” Sissel exclaimed. “You are right. I’ve been a coward, not wanting to face Runeard. He scares me. But not as much as the idea of our lands being destroyed. Our people deserve better.”

“So you’re going to talk to him?” Inger asked, her voice rising in hope.

“Yes. We’ll go back to Arendelle together, and I’ll request another audience. I’m going to tell him Vesterland will not contribute to this project.”

“And without our funding, he’ll never get it off the ground!” Inger crowed. “Take that, Runeard.” She raised a fist triumphantly, swinging her arm in the air as if punching their grandfather in the nose. Elsa started to laugh. She liked this girl!

But the laughter died in her throat as a noise rose in her ears. The roar of approaching water.

“A flash flood,” Elsa gasped. “There was a flash flood.”

No sooner had she said the words than it came into view. Rushing water racing down the river at top speed. Sissel screamed in horror. She leapt backward.

“Inger!” she cried. Her sister was right in the path of the water.

Inger’s face turned white, but she didn’t move. It was as if she was frozen by fear.

“Inger!” Sissel tried again. Her voice was full of panic. She dove for her sister, throwing herself at her, knocking her out of the water’s path. But her foot caught on a root, and she tripped, falling into the water.

“Sissel!” Inger screamed. “No!”

Inger scrambled to her feet, dashing to the riverbank. Sissel was already far away, thrashing in the water just as Elsa had been doing moments before. With the water rougher because of the flood, waves rose over the shore, forcing Inger to stumble backward and further away.

“Inger!” Sissel cried. “Help me, Inger!” She tried to grab hold of a fallen log, then some outstretched branches—anything to stop from being pulled away. Meanwhile, Inger ran alongside the shore, screaming for help.

Elsa glanced at Anna, then started to run down the river, following the vision. Suddenly, she stopped short, her eyes bulging from her head as she realized what Sissel was headed for.

A giant waterfall.

“Look out, Sissel!” Inger cried, her face streaming with tears as she ran helplessly along the shore. “Look out!”

Sissel glanced behind her, her jaw dropping as she realized what was coming. She lunged for the shore again, this time managing to grab on to a small branch. She struggled to use it as a rope to pull herself to shore. But the current was too strong and the branch began to crack.

At that moment the vision froze, crystallizing into solid ice. Elsa frowned, trying to push more magic into it, to get it moving again. But it was stuck fast as if paused on purpose.

She looked back at the draugr, who was still standing there by its statue. But this time the creature’s eyes weren’t on the two sisters by the river. It was looking at something behind them.

Or make that…someone.

“Look!” Anna cried, pointing. “Who’s that?”

Elsa squinted at the figure, standing motionless, encased in ice. It appeared to be a young boy—around fourteen or fifteen years of age. He had shaggy hair and big eyes and was carrying a shepherd’s crook. In fact, she realized, as her eyes dropped lower, there was a lamb at his feet.

“Whoa,” she whispered.

“It’s the witness!” Anna cried. “From Kristoff’s story! I totally forgot until now, but he said there was a witness! That’s how they were able to prove Inger’s crime!” She turned back to Elsa. “Make the memory move again. Let’s see if he says anything.”

Elsa bit her lower lip. “Um, I didn’t stop it to begin with.” She glanced over at the draugr. “Can you show us more?”

The creature seemed to nod. The vision leapt back to life. Inger’s screams once again reached their ears.

“Help me!” she was crying to the boy. “Help me save my sister! Please!”

“Stay where you are,” the boy shouted. “You’ll be swept away, too!” He ran to the shore, leaning over the water, wrapping his hand around a tree to anchor himself. He tried to grab the other end of the branch Sissel was clinging to, but it was just out of his reach. Inger stood watching, helpless and scared.

“Come on, Sissel,” she whispered. “Just hold on.”

Sissel looked up at her younger sister. Her brown eyes no longer reflected her fear, but rather a strange sense of resolve. Elsa cringed, realizing the truth. At that very moment, Sissel had known she was going to die. And she had accepted her fate.

“I love you, Inger,” Sissel said. “And I believe in you. I know you will do me proud.”

“NO!” Inger begged, her face twisted with horror. “Don’t leave me, Sissel!” Her voice cracked on the words. “I can’t do this without you!”

But her sister only shook her head. “Yes, you can,” she said solemnly. Her voice no longer sounded afraid, but determined. “You can do anything.” She paused, then added, “You’re my sister. And you’re stronger than you know.”

And with that, the branch broke free. Sissel’s body was tossed like a rag doll over the falls. Inger screamed in agony, collapsing to the ground, sobs wracking her body.

“Sissel,” she cried out. “Oh, my sweet Sissel.”

A moment later the shepherd boy was by her side. He tried to help her get up, but Inger’s legs refused to work. She kept staring at the raging river, her whole body trembling with grief. The boy reached down, gently swiping a lock of hair from her face, meeting her eyes with his own.

“What’s your name?” he said gently.

“Inger,” she whispered, clinging to his hand.

He nodded. “Inger, I’m Stig. I’m going to help you,” he said.

And just like that, the vision faded. The raging river went quiet again.

Elsa turned slowly back to the draugr. It was still standing by the shore, staring at the water. It took Elsa a moment to realize the creature’s cheeks were wet.

It was crying. She was crying.

“Your sister didn’t murder you,” Anna whispered. “That’s what you’ve been trying to tell us, isn’t it? Everyone’s been spreading a false story! You want them to know the truth. It was an accident. Your sister was innocent all along. She loved you. And you loved her.”

Sissel nodded, staring forlornly at the river. Elsa felt her heart go out to the creature, and suddenly she half wanted to run over and give her a warm hug. They’d been afraid of the draugr for so long. But now she felt only pity as she gazed on the grotesque creature. For Inger, too, who had been accused of a crime she hadn’t committed. To lose your sister like that had to feel like you’d lost one of your own limbs. Elsa could only hope this was a pain she’d never have to go through herself.

Because to lose Anna…her Anna…

She shook her head. No. She wouldn’t even think of it. She couldn’t.

Elsa looked up at the draugr again. “You were trying to share this memory with me earlier, weren’t you?” she asked, realization washing over her. “When we met you in the forest. You grabbed my hand. I thought you were trying to erase my memories. But you were trying to share your own.” She gave an apologetic shrug. “I’m sorry I didn’t understand.”

The draugr shuffled from foot to foot, moaning softly. Elsa decided to take that as forgiveness. She turned back to Anna.

“At least now we know the whole story,” she said. “What really happened.”

“Do we, though?” Anna asked, scratching her head as she looked from the draugr to the memorial upstream. “Why did Inger get blamed for it all? I mean, there was a witness! Why didn’t she and that boy, Stig, just go back and tell people what really happened? Her name would have been cleared!”

Sissel moaned, shaking her head. She clearly didn’t know why—she had died before that part of the story happened. Leaving yet another mystery to solve, Elsa realized. Just one more mystery in this whole thing.

“Don’t worry,” she told Sissel. “We’re going to figure this out. Somehow. And then we’ll tell everyone the truth. What really happened. Clear your sister’s name once and for all.”

The draugr’s eyes seemed to brighten. “Sissssster,” she moaned, seeming to agree. “Sissssster mine…” And with that, she began to shuffle off into the woods.

Elsa and Anna watched her go, amazed.

“Guess we know what the draugr wants now,” Anna said.

“And we know where to go next,” Elsa agreed. “To find the one person who might still be alive. The one person who was really there.”

“Stig,” Anna said. “And I know just how to track him down.”

赫尔加的地图，事实证明，并不算精确无误。

事实上，他们在漆黑的树林里迷路了三次，才终于跌跌撞撞地走到那座简陋的小木像前——那是立在河湾石座上、纪念维斯特兰两位公主的雕像。

艾莎欢快地指了指它，安娜长舒一口气，翻身跳下哈夫斯基，冲了过去。

她双手叉腰，打量着雕刻的木头。"你看，说不定西塞尔只是想要一座新纪念碑呢，"她戳着本该是西塞尔手臂的位置说道。

显然这些年里它某处断裂过，有些木头已经烂透了。"我是说，这座都快散架了。""要是真有那么简单就好了。"艾莎笑着从水马背上滑下，走到安娜身边。

她眯起眼睛看着那座木碑，它显然已风光不再。

她想，任凭风吹雨打五十年，再结实的木头也免不了这样。

不过，底部的刻字还算清晰，能看得清。

"至爱公主。"

"愿你们安息。"

但愿她们能如愿——而且越快越好。"这绝对就是我在幻象里看到的地方，"艾莎若有所思地说，目光投向湍急的水流。"我记得离岸边那块大石头。

"那棵树现在大多了，但当时肯定就在那儿，"她补充道，指着河上方垂着枝条的一棵大橡树。

她点点头。"对，这里就是西塞尔溺亡的确切地点。""可那是英格干的吗？"安娜问。"这才是我们需要解答的问题。

"如果真是她——又为什么要这么做？"

"到目前为止，我们了解到的一切都表明姐妹俩感情很好。"

"她们彼此相爱。""没错。

"我是说，她们固然在一些事上有分歧，但那又怎样呢？"艾莎反问。"咱们不也整天意见不合吗。""通常都是因为你让自己陷进危险，"安娜指出。

艾莎嗤笑一声。

她转回身对着纪念碑。"在阿托哈兰的幻象里，我看见西塞尔在水中挣扎。

"但我们需要回溯到更早之前。

"去听清她们当时在争执什么，又发生了什么。

"只有这样才能确凿地知道真相。"她转向河流。

河水湍急地从他们身边奔涌而过，激流卷起大块的浮冰。

和流经阿伦黛尔镇中心那段他们熟悉的平缓宁静的水面大不相同。

艾莎猜测附近或许有座冰川，用融雪为河流补给水量。

即便水性再好的人，在那里也难把头露出水面。

她把手探进河里，用手指感受着水流。"你感觉到什么了吗？"安娜急切地问。

艾莎摇摇头。"只有刺骨的冰水，"她皱着眉回答。

她闭上眼睛，想着西塞尔和英格。

努力想象她们在这岸边的模样。

争吵着。

她们在吵些什么？

可她什么也没感觉到。

直到这时她才意识到问题所在。

水是有记忆的。

但这股特别的水流，已不是西塞尔溺亡时停留在这里的那片水了。

河水始终在流动，永远在变化。

如果艾莎身在阿托哈兰，或许能借助记忆之灵的力量，翻找出些什么。

但在这里——只能靠她自己，她没把握能成功。

艾莎一屁股坐在河岸边，满心沮丧。

如果她的魔力帮不上任何人的忙，那又有什么用？

难道这一切都是死路一条？

一股挫败感在她心底升起。

她攥紧双手成拳。"喂！

"艾莎！

"放松点。"她感到安娜来到身边，用双臂搂住她。"没事的。""这根本不好！"艾莎厉声说。"我得把这件事查清楚！"她挣脱安娜的怀抱，再次把双手浸入刺骨的冰水中。

也许潜得更深些，她就能找到些什么。

她紧紧闭上眼睛。

努力着，努力着。

"扑通！"

艾莎失去平衡，一头栽进冰冷的河里，惊声尖叫。

她拼命扑腾，想用脚抵住滑溜的石头，却被一口脏水呛得喘不过气。

水流湍急，飞快把她往下游拖。"安娜！"她喊道，试图用魔力冻结奔涌的河水。

可什么事也没发生。

就好像她戴着手套似的——尽管她并没有戴。

大概是探得太深耗尽了魔力，如今它们又快要熄灭了。

"哦，不。

"不，不，不！"安娜！

"救命！"她又喊了一声，知道自己听起来很惊恐。

绝望极了。

她拼命把头露出水面，抓住空当拼命吸气。

可恰恰相反，她大口吞着河水，呛得连连咳嗽，又再次想探到河底。

可这里水很深，她的脚只是徒劳地乱蹬，水流把她往更深处拽。

她的身体开始发软。
